1.--TAE FORTE I:IRIDGR. When the wild men from Pentland's, shaggy side Stared at the Fifeshire woodlands, did they dream This fiery dragon with its inner; of steam Would make the heaven its pathway, and would glide With cloud and sound above the wondering tide? Could they have hoped hot Haste would drive Its team Straight for the gulf, and leap you ocean stream, High o'er Inchgarvie's isle, with double strid? Nay, but the I ciart of iron was In the land, The soul of fire, the strength of lifted arm; The breath of wind was theirs: one thing alone They knew not—this—how God Himself had planned Mortals should conquer Earth, and bind in one Our broken world, with commerce for a charm. ll.—Tag Etym. TOWER. The men who builded Babel, day by day Saw the great city less, the plains more wide, Till God sent down confusion for their pride, And tower and french sank back to common clay. Nor better fared the wen who far away Beheld their harbour giant o'er the tide, For lo! earth trembled, and the people cried, And Rhodos' Colossus crashed into the bay. But this transcendent tower of magic birth, That tames the lightning-flash and mocks the thunder. Has set a star in Heaven—with upturned eyes The nations meet, and pass in marvel under. And humbled, in the silence of surprise They .find a long-lost language of the earth. 11. D. RAWNSLEY. —Blackwood's Magazine, for March.

'rime may be money, but most men wilt' stand at a street corner for an bdur, waiting tor a 'ha or tramcar rather than pay for a cab. A party of college students once brought to their lec- turing professor a beetle, cunningly manufactured of 'thread and wire, asking him to tell them to what species it belonged. After a long scrutiny he said, "Gentlemen I believe that this belongs to the genus humbug." An English lady of great beauty and attraction, who was an ardent admirer of Ireland, crowned her praises of it at a party by saying, "I think I was meant for an Irishwoman." "Cross the Channel, madam," said Lover, who was present, "and millions would say that you were meant for an Irishman."

Digestion will not begin till the temperature of the food has been raised by the heat of the stomach to 98degs- Hence the more heat that can be imparted to it by slow mastication the better. The precipitation of a large quantity of cold food into the stomach by fast eating may, and often does, cause discomfort and indigestion, and every occasion of this kind results in a measurable injury to the digestive function. Ice water drunk with cold food of course increases the mischief. Hot drinks —hot water, weak tea, coffee, chocolate, &c.—will, on the contrary, help to prevent it. But eat slowly, any way. 'lnn STORY OF SIR HENRY WYA.T.—Sir: Henry had been a faithful supporter of the King before he attained the throne, and had consequently been "imprisoned often; once in a cold and narrow tower, where he had neither bed to lie on nor clothes sufficient to warm him, nor meat for his mouth. He had starved there had not God, who sent a crow (raven?) to feed his prophet, sent this His and his country's martyr a cat both to feed and warm him. It was his own relation unto them from whom I had it. A cat came one day down into the dungeon unto him and, as it were, offered herself unto -him. He was glad of her, laid her in his bosom to warm him, and, by making much of her, won her love. After this she would come every day unto him divers times and, when she could get one, bring him a pigeon. Be complained to his keeper of his cold and short fare. The answer was, durst not better it.' • But,' said Sir Henry, if I can provide any, will you promise to dress it for me?' 'I may well enough,' said he, the keeper; 'you are safe for that matter.' And, being urged again, promised him, and kept his promise— dressed for him from time to time such pigeons as his accator the cat provided for him. Sir Henry Wyat in his prosperity for this would ever 'make much of cats, as other men will of their spaniels or hounds ; and per- haps you shall not find his picture any where but, like Sir Christopher Hatton with his dog, with a cat before him."—The Women's World for March. WELSHMEN Bisizors in ENGLAND.—A quandary on space will permit but a brief reference to the many bishops whom Wales gave to England. It is somewhat noteworthy that there should be at one time two con- temporaries bearing the name of William Lloyd—both Welshmen. At another time there were three, almost contemporaneous, bearing the name of John Thomas, while a fourth named William Thomas lived but a short time before. Two of the four Thomasses are known to be Welshmen. William, after having been consecrated to St. David's, became Bishop of:Worcester. One of his frequent sayings was that no bishop or prisst was to enrich himself or raise his family with the revenues of the Church, because that was against the sacred canons. One of the deans of Worcester, Dr. Hickes, speaks of him in an extant letter as "that excellent bishop worthy of everlasting memory." Of the three Johns, one was suc- cessively Bishop of St. Asaph. Lincoln, and Salisbury; another of Peterborough, Salisbury. and Winchester; the third, of Rochester. All three had held: livings in the city. The first and third had both been Royal chap- lains, and the second had been preceptor to George 111. There is an anecdote that some one was speaking of Dr. Thomas. "Which Dr. Thomas do you mean?" "Dr. John Thomas." "They are both named John." "Dr. Thomas who had a living in the city." "They have both livings in the eitv." "Dr. Thomas who is a chap- lain to the king.' '"They are both chaplains to the king." " Dr. Thomas who is a very good preacher." They are both very good preachers." "Dr. Thomas who squints." "They both squint."—Newbery House Xagactne.

THE COLLAPSE OP THE CHARTIST AGITATION IN 1848. —Only two rears have passed since the invasion of the flouses of Parliament by Feargus O'Connor sod his Chartist hordes had been averted by the genius and determination of the Great Captain. When the Queen agent to Osborne, and the Duke of Wellington accepted the command of all the forces, it was understood that be was to possess undivided responsibility and authority. It was truly a momentous day when in the very early dawn a large force was concentrated in the metropolis, and yet not a soldier to be seen the whole day; not a carriage was seen in the streets, which were only patrolled by special constables. at four o'clock, when the House was sitting, Feargus O'Connor asked permission for the Chartist delegates from the mass on the other side of Westminster Bridge to introduce the monster petition. The answer was, that the petition of the people would, of course, be received by the House, but no deputation. Then Feargus O'Connor's heart sank. On the Vauxhall aide of the bridge, there were tho tens of thousands be bad collected from all parts in the hope of the plunder of the metropolis; but O'Connor well knew that although no soldier was seen, they occupied every house in the vicinity; that the Great Duke had said, if one of his soldiers was struck with a stone, or a man put his foot on the bridge, the leaders of the movement and their followers must take the consequences of their deeds. The connon knew no distinction of persons, DO Feargus O'Connor took the most prudent course, and with great difficulty tnduced his forces to disperse, and so ended the eventful revolution of 1848.—/a the Dovs of the Iliendieg. in Black-wood's Magazine for March, 1890. WHELAN inc THE SPlTTOONS.—Britannia, who shops with us this June morning in Boston, gases meditatively about the floors. "Where are the spittoons?' she mur- murs as dulcetly as though she asked, " What are the wild waves saying ?" "Spittoons?" "Are not heaps of these shop-people, men and women, chewing gum with might and main," There was no "denigin of it." Chew. thew, chew—" sales-gentlemen" and "sales-ladies" alike. Their jaws worked like automatic machines. We con- fessed then and there to Britannia that this habit of chew- ing is a really national one. Our chewers are in every rank of life, in every profession. Last summer, at the C— House on Reach Bluff-hy-the-Sea, it was a spec- taole to see faultlessly attired men and women upon the broad piazzas swaying for ever back and forth in rocking-chairs, chewing, chewing, ever chewing, though the eternal tides came in or the eternal tides went out; though Xolian music swept up from the great deep, or dusty zephyrs howled out from the wide land. Strange was it to hear a beauteous bride call from halfway up the stairs to her husband below, "Arthur, I do wish you would look under the seat of my rocker, and see if I didn't leave my gum there !" So popular is this gum habit that physicians have been known to advise it for gastric deficiencies, as aid to the salivary flow. In its first condition this gum is a hard lump, difficult to mani- pulate. Not until it has been pretty thoroughly chewed is it agreeably chewable. For this reason the first chew- ing is something to be avoided, if possible; and a cer- tain well-known figure, a boarder in a certain well- known. hotel, is said to maintain his high popularity by preparing their gum for all his women-friends ! Cassell's Magazine.

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.

Mr. Herbert Gladstone has been laid up with a sharp attack of influenza, but rose from his bed On Monday night and gallantly went down to the house to vote for his father's amendment. He was none of the worse on Tuesday for kis rather risky experiment.

The epidemic some time ago raised the price of quinine. It is now reported from Rotherham that the demand for medicine bottles is unusually acute. In reply to the old question, "Where do the pins all go to?" it was once alleged gravely that mil- liners swallowed them,for the speaker had seen them sticking out of the girls' mouths. Patients cannot swallow the bottles as well as the medicine.

A number of Gladstonian Liberals in London have set on foot a proposal to entertain all the Parnellite members of the House of Commons at a banquet some time before the close of the Parliamentary session. An effort will be made to obtain a hall in the metropolis capable of accommodating thousand diners.

It is not true, as stated by a weekly contempor- ary, that Sir William Harcourt refused to dine with the Speaker on Wednesday week on account of any personal disagreement between them. Mr.Ponsonby accidentally mislaid Sir Willifun Harcourt's card of invitation, and by the time the error was discovered Sir William had arranged to leave town that after- noon.

The warmth of the Egyptian climate has already had a beneficial effect upon Lord Hartington, who is looking much better since his illness, and has been going about Cairo, riding, walking, and driv- ing, as if be had never been ill. He was received in audience by his Highness the Khedive, and spent several mornings with Sir Evelyn Baring. . Lord Hartington started up the Nile on the Ist inst.

A quasi-official intimation has been made that the Bishop of Truro will return to England next montlhand that he is then to decide whether he will resign the see. It is indeed full time that Bishop Wilkinson either resigned or resumed his duties. lie has now been absent from England for nearly a year, and he had previously been an invalid, and usually away from the diocese, for about fifteen months. It is really scandalous.

The crisis in the ranks of the Commission on Sweating is complete, and Lord Dunraven, the ckairman has sent in his resignation. Lord Dunraven makes no secret of his conviction that his report has been thrown out from a suspicion that he and Lord Randolph Churchill have contrived it between them to snap up the labour vote throughout the country. As a matter of fact, Lord Randolph Churchill has had nothing to do with the report.

There is some talk in Rochdale of keeping Mr. T. B. Potter's seat open for Mr. W. L. Bright, should the latter gain sufficient health to again seek Parliamentary honours,and should Hr. Potter retire. Hr. Potter was the pet friend of John Bright. He has for some time rented Richard Cobden's cottage at ilidhurst, amid Cobden's associations and sur- rounded by his books and papers, as well as by other people's reminiscences of the great free trader.

The Prince of Wsles went to and returned from Scotland last week in a new saloon, which has been built by the Great Northern expressly for Royal travellers by the East Coast ronte, and which is a marvel of comfort and convenience. The carriage includes a sitting-room, two bedrooms, a smoking compartment, lavatories, kitchen, with cooking apparatus, and accommodation for servants, and is heated throughout with hot water, and lighted by electricity. The decorations are very pretty, and the furniture perfect.

A rather amusing incident happened on the Prince's arrival at Dalmeny Station. The train arrived two or three minutes before its time, and on stopping at the station there was no carriages or anyone to meet the Royal party, and the Prince, after getting ready to alight, was obliged to go back and wait until Lord Rosebery arrived some minutes later, when the party drove off to Dalmeny. The Scotch papers say some wae. in the crowd kept cal- ling on the Prince for "Three cheers for Glad- stone." to which appeal he laughingly shook his head.

A lady, name unknown, has taken decisive steps to reform the administration of justice in Texas. Enterino. the Mayor's Court at Gainesville, where her husband had been subjected to the indignity of a fine, she knocked down first a policeman, next the City Attorney, and finally the Mayor. She next thrashed them all and drove them out of the court, of which she retained possession for three hours. She is described as weighing seventeen stone, and "her victims are much disfigured about the face." Mrs. Weldon must look to her laurels.

When the Queen leaves for the Continent,. which according to the most recent arrangements, will be on Monday week, the 24th inst., her Majesty will be accompanied by Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg, and tbe suit will consist of Lady Churchill, General Sir if. F. Ponsenhy, the lion. Harriet Phipps, Major Bigge, and Dr. Reid. The Queen travels by special train over the South Wes- tern Railway to Portsmouth, and crosses the English Channel in the Victoria and Albert yacht to Cherbourg. Aix les Bains will be reached on Wed- nesday, the 26th inst., and the Royal party will drive immediately to the Maison 3lottet.

The Queen is fond of her Sunday drive. At half- past four the quiet carriage and the spiritless grey horses come round to the private apartments, and the mournful procession starts off, with the melan- choly outrider in advance. The liveries are jet black, and the dour Scot by the coachman's side does little to brighten the scene. The Queen drove through Old Windsor, on Sunday afternoon, to the astonishment of two Americans, who could scarcely believe that the lady in the white shawl, shielding herself from the cold wind with a black parasol, was the Queen.

The "Pall Mall Gazette's" story about Canon Udder' preaching before the Queen is full of blun- ders. The sermon was not delivered in the St. George's Chapel but in the private chapel at Windsor Castle. Canon Liddon offended the Queen by suddenly addressing her in an eloquent and solemn passage cribbed (or "adapted," let us say) from one of the great French preachers of the last century. He commenced "And thou, 0 Queen must also die." whereupon her Majesty drew th curtain, which then hung above the Royal!' Gallery and was seen no more UV the preacher/ It is all very well to talk of "sinking the courtier in the priest," but an effective sermon could surely have been preached by Canon Liddon witbbut his per- sonally addressing her Majesty in so unpleasant and unprecedented a fashion.

Dr. Richardson admits that since he first warned us of the dangers of immoderate cycling, changes have taken place in the construction both of bicycles and tricycles which materially, modify the old drawbacks. He is still however of Opinion that cycling should never be practiced by boys and girls sillce it differs from other exercises in the fact that •• •

it moulds the bodily framework, as it were, to its own mode of motion: and riders in course of time almost invariably acquire what he •calls "the cyclist's figure," which is not graceful r and is not indicative of the possession of perfectly balanced power.

At a recent meeting-of the London County Coun- cil a registered letter was put into the hands of Mr. John Burns. It bore the postmark of Ballarat, Australia, and further examination showed that it was addressed as follows: " Mr. John Birns, leader of the Dock Strike, care of Editor of the "Times," London." On the other aide was written in pencil, " Refused at "Times "office." The letter had been returned to the Postoffice. and had been pursuing Mr. Burns for some days, eventually running him to earth at the County Council meeting. It con- tained a cheque for £5OO, being the balance of the contribution from the Trade Hall Council at Ballarat.

Kangaroos are said to be thriving on one of Lord Rothschild's estates, and the publication of the fact has brought to light the circumstance. that their introduction is not the absolute novelty which many persons would have supposed. At Sidraouth, in Surrey, a gentleman kept—if he does not still keep —some of these animals; and at Beeaton Hill, Cheshire, a landmark familiar to passengers by the London and 5 orth-Westem Railway, it is said that the kangaroo is, to all intents and purposes, actually acclimatised. Elsewhere some were turned out, but poisoned themselves by eating laurel. They seem to find food for themselves, however, and will appar- ently live if poisonous shrubs are carefully removed from their haunts.

" Father " Ignatius has now assumed the more exalted title of "Abbot.' On St. David's Day his church was illuminated with 200 wax candles and innumerable small tapers, and three new monks were received into the community. The "Abbot' was gorgeously apparelled in cloth of gold,'" and the new monks having taken a vow of celibacy, obedience, and poverty, laid on their backs on the floor, ,of the church.' A funeral pall was placed over them, and the ." Abbot " read the Burial Service. A black curtain was next drawn across the church, hiding everything from the con- gregation, and when it was withdrawn it was seen that the head of each was encircled with a wreath. It is evident that, notwithstanding the recent rumour of his death, there is still plenty of life in " Father " Ignatius.

div.head: SOW TO AVOID A COLD.
div.p: SOW TO AVOID A COLD.
BY ONE WllO DOES.

The above is the title of a racily-written pamphlet, issued by Messts. Griffith, Farren, and Co., Loudon. We append two chapters by way of showing the quality of the author. It will be seen that, along with plenty of good advice, there is no lack of good fun.

div.head: NOSE AND ITS DUTIES.
div.p: THE NOSE AND ITS DUTIES.

Most people have noses of one shape or another, and many suppose that the principal function of this prominent organ is smell. This is erroneous. The big-nosed wolf in the fairy tale, misrepresented the duty of his snout in his well-known reply to little Red Riding Hood. The nose is given us chiefly to breathe with, and one of its responsibilities is to warn its owner of the approach of catarrh. The first symptom of cold in the head is usually an unpleasant titillation at the upper part of the nose, provocative of sneezing. This sensation is due to what doctors call "raft; nervous action." The more often you visit the modern physician, the greater your chance of falling in with reflexes; although, to speak precisely, the angle of incidence is not always equal to the bent of your after- reflection, when fees are payable. .Rhinitia is an irritation of the inside of the nose.

The use of this word is by no means restricted to the owners of Grecian noses, although its deriva- tion might lead a classical scholar to assume this to be the case. The inhalation of street-dust is a fruitful source of rhinitis. Hence men naturally display anxiety to lay the dust. "Down with the dust" is a proverbial say- ing amongst sporting men whose transactions take them much in the open air. Of all sequels to a surgical operation, perhaps that of paying for it tbrough the nose is one of the most objectionable. To avoid so doing, refrain from breathing dusty air; otherwise both your nose and your pocket will suffer from the indiscretion. _

Remember the bonds of your connection with the rhino and with rhinktis are inversely propor- tioned as to strength. The closer the latter adheres to the lining of the nose, the less the former is likely to stick to the lining of your pocket. Another duty of the healthy nose is to warm the air in its passage to the lungs. By the chinks and crannies in its curled and twisted membranes the air is split up into small currents and eddies which quickly attain the tetn- perature of the body. It is unnecessary to possess an unduly red and heated organ for this purpose. Any nose is good enough to breathe with, pro- vided it is pervious to the passage of air. When there are reasons to believe that, a school- boy, for instance, does not respire through his nos- trils, request him to say his catechism. If in reply to the first query, he answers Eb or Ed (M or N being the nasal consonants selected by the rubric), do not at once assume that his father is a Nonconformist; believe rather that the child is a mouth-breather, and take his measure accordingly. The nose also acts as an air-filter.

The smoke and duet which happy cockneys inhale during their daily perambulations through the met- ropolis are mostly retained in the nostrils to their subsequent discomfort. Blow your nose frequently for many reasons. Amongst others you may so ascertain whether it is pervious. If it is not, you can still indulge mentally in the expletives "Blow it they soothe the mind. It is unnecessary, however, "To wake the echoes with resounding blows," whenever you indulge in a kerchief performance. Learn to use the implement daintily, yet withal effectually.

THE MOTITII AND ITS ABUSE. This chapter does not consist of a dissertation upon the language of Billingsgate, altinugh the idea is fascinating. The subject is, however, too vast for the present -treatise to deal with. The preceding chapter opened with some remarks upon•On nose, the present one is immediately con- cerned in the closure of the mouth.
_ For respiratory purposes the mouth is a failure. We learn this from the frog. Keep its mouth open, and it soon dies or dries. The result is the same to the frog in either case.
"Shut your mouth" ought to be written on the lintels of each house (of Legislature) in the king- dom.

Many good reasons can generally be adduced for closing the jaws, none for keeping them perman- ently separated. Better conform literally to the vulgar precept, and evor "hold your jaw," than wander through life with the mouth open. "Speech is silvem ; Silence is golden," says the philosopher; and quietude is never more precious than at dusk. 7,

To sleep comlortably one. Must breathe through the nose; else bath the sleeper and his auditors are profoundly disturbed, the one by alternate fits of choking, snorting. and gasping ; the others by envy and bitterness of spirit at the sonorous cause of their wakefulness.

--When the mist rises and the dew falls, then let us close our mouths tightly lest we rue it. Our snc.rts and our snuffles, our sneezes and snores are obtained from the same source as fog, sleet, and sludge, and bespeak a northern ancestry versed in these climatic phenomena. On the other hand, the Roman soldiery in Ceesar's time, could not have snored loudly, else that great general would not have repeatedly recorded a march out of camp silentio noetis. It would be interesting te learn how far the linguistic peculiarities of a race are moulded by its susceptibility to colds in the held. The pronunciation of the gutturals and sibilants of the Teuton and Sclav is unaffected by the cir- cumstance that the speaker may be'suffering from nasal catarrh.

The melodious tones of Italy, Spain. and many other Celtic nations can only be produced by gene- rations of men accustomed to inhabit lands where the air is soft and warm, and conducive to indolence rather than to obstruction of the nose..
Great singers are necessarily nose-breathers; and we find Italian of all languages lends itself most readily and naturally to the intonations of a tuneful voice.
When we take our morning (or evening) walks abroad let us look to our mouths. By their closure We keep the lining membrane moist.

div.head: DARESBURY HIGHWAY .BOARD.
div.p: DARESBURY HIGHWAY .BOARD.
A special meeting of this Board was held at Daresbury on Monday. Mr. Cliffs presided, and there was a good attendance of members.

RESIGNATION OF THE SURVEYOR.—A letter was read from Mr. Pearman, the Surveyor, resigning his position, he having been appointed one of the main road inspec- tors under the Cheshire County Council.—Mr. W. PIER- POINT suggested that they might by advancing Mr. Pearman's salary induce him to remain in the service of the Board. He had always been struck with the care and attention Mr. Pearman gave to his duties, and it was hardly desirable to lose a good officer. Their surveyor now received £l5O a year and if they increased that to £2OO it would be as much as he was going to get from the County Council.—Mr. JOHN HAR.BYSHIRE mentioned that the surveyor of the Board would hereafter have 1014 miles of main roads taken from under his care, and therefore it seemed rather an opportunity for reducing the salary than raising it.—Mr. HADDOCK spoke in com- plimentary language of the way the surveyor had attended to his duties, and strongly supported the sug- gestion of Mr. Pierpoint.—Mr. AARON spoke to the tame effect. He believed in paying men salaries with which they would he satisfied, and he had had more men under him than probably any other member of that Board.— Mr. J. Mits.:sums : Hear, hear.—Mr. AARON repeated the statement.—Mr. DAnursiturn : Hear, hear.—Mr. ' AARON: I am on my feet.—Mr. HARBYSIIIRR : Hear, hoar. —Mr. AARos ; And you shut your mouth. (Much laugh- ter.)—MX. CLARKE moved that the surveyor's salary be raised to £l7O and that he be asked to withdraw his re- signation.—This proposition having been seconded, a pro- posal was also made that the resignation be accepted. On being put to the vote the latter proposal was carried by 12 votes to six. It was decided to advertise for a new surveyor at a salary of £l5O a year. TRH LATCHFORD Bninoes.—The CLERE stated that one of the objects for which that meeting had been called was "to reconsider, and if necessary, to rescind the reso- lutions come to at the last meeting with reference to the roads and bridges over and adjacent to the Ship Canal in Latchford, or elsewhere." Mr. J. C. PARR, in introduc- ing the discussion on this subject, spoke of a letter he had written in which it was stated that the Parliamentary Committee of the County Council had decided to oppose the present proposal of the Ship Canal Company as it affected the diversion of Knutsferd-road where it crossed I the canal, that they considered a permaneat high ' level vehicular bridge much preferable to swing bridges as now projected, and that they were prepared to appoint certain members of their Committee to advise with the Daresbury Dlghway Board in the mattes with a view to united action. He (Mr. Parr) thought the decision of the Local Government Board to have the goods station as well as the passenger station at Latchford on a high level would materially alter the view of the Highway Board with regard to the proposal as to a high level vehicular bridge. The Parliamentary Committee of the County Council having had the plans of the Ship Canal Company before them, unanimously, he believed, decided to oppose them in consequence of the diversion of Kuutsferd-road. The Commit- tee wished to see the spot and they asked him (Mr. Parr) to meet them there which he did. There were present Mr. Lister the chairman of the Committee, Mr. Earpe, • and two others, together with Mr. Bull, the eotmty surveyor, and one of the engineers of the Ship Canal. They went carefully into the matter and their objection to the diversion of Knutsford-road, was strengthened, as well as their desire to have a vehicular bridge. There was one other point he should like to refer to. He saw that at the last meeting a member asked how long the swing bridges could be kept open, and the reply was three minutes. He should, however, like to point out that the words of the Act were that the bridges should not be longer than three minutes in open- ing or closing, but the time they might be kept open was entirely undefined. The only remedy was that if the time was considered unreasonable the matter might be brought before a justice of the peace, but to his mind that was very unsatisfactory. If it took a vessel five minutes to get past, there would be a delay of eleven minutes, and if there happened to be two vessels, or one going each way the delay might be very great. He con- sidered it was very desirable to have a high level vehicu- lar bridge, and he moved that the resolutions previously passed lce, the Board with regard to this matter be res- cinded.—lt was here pointed out that the resolutions referred to were not passed at the last mooting and therefore could not be rescinded at that special meeting, which had been called to "rescind reso.utions come to at the last meeting."—Mr. J. C. PARR said he was sorry if he had made a mistake in the wording of the requisi- tion. That was a matter of very great importance and he had no personal interest to serve in any shape or way. They had that day an opportunity of doing a great service to the public which might not again occur.—Mr. T. HALL thought they ought to have more information before being asked to proceed further,and plans ought to be submitted. Ile was of opinion that the swing bridge in Acker's-lane was of as much importance as the high level bridge.—Mr. W. PIERPOINT asked as to the gradient of the proposed high level bridge, and he expressed sur- prise that the County Council had gene out of their way in order to interfere in that matter at all, as the only road that effected them was the Knutsford-road.—Mr. C. Lister (chairman of the Parliamentary Committee of the County Council), Mr. S. Ball (county surveyor), were then vaned into the room, and they explained cer- tain plans which were laid upon the table. They were subsequently joined by Mr. Hunter and Mr. 0. G. Breekes,erepneers representing the Ship Canal Company,l when the plans were further explained.—Mr. Hoarse, In answer to a question, said the goods station at I Latchford would be constructed on the same level as the passenger station.—Mr. PIERPOINT said he had been assured that the low level goods station would be retained. He should now have to cart his goods to Warrington for he would not have them taken up a gradient of 1 in 25. —Mr. litorres said he only knew the arrangements that had been entered into between the L. Is N.-W. Railway Company and the Ship Canal Company. Un- less the Canal Company could meet the wishes of the local authorities with regard to the bridges they should have to fall back upon their old plans of 1885.—Mr. Joins HARETSITIRR said they wented a swing bridge at Ackers- lane, one at Knuteford-road, and one at Twenty-step Bridge, and it was only reasonable that those should be provided.—Mr. TRostes HALL: We want a bridge at ackers-lane. certainly. Mr. llusrrea We will not make a high level bridge, and a swing bridge at Ackers-lane. Mr. PIHRTOINT : Then that settles the matter.—The CLARK read a letter which had been received from Mr. Wm. Long, who said he hoped the members of the Board would require very good and substantial reasons before they consented to rescind or interfere with the decision arrived at previously as to the arrangement of roads and bridges over the canal at Latchford, which was acquiesced in by the County Sur- veyor,the Ship Canal authorities,and the Board, and was acceptable to a large majority of the Latchford residents, as being on the whole the best that could be come to. (Hear, hear.)—.Mr. J. C. PARR said the feeling in Latch- ford was so divided that it was impossible for Mr. Long to say what really the view of Latchford was.—Mr. W. PIERPOINT said the real view of Latchford was that they wanted the scheme as at present before Parliament adopted.—Mr. J. C. PARR moved "That this Board appoint a Committee to confer with the Parliamentary Committee of the County Council with reference to the proposed alterations of the roads at Latchford and Grap- penhall from the deposited plans previously approved by the Board, atid that a Committee have power to settle the matter."—Mr. BURGESS seconded.—Mr. W. Pisßeoner moved an amendment that the scheme as approved by. the Highway Board be adopted according to the deposited plans.—This was seconded by Mr. JoRN DARBYSHIRE.— Four members voted for Mr. Parr's motion and four for I the amendment, and the former was carried by the cast- ing vote of the Chairman. It was, however, after some further discussion decided to adjourn the meeting till that day week to await the receipt of amended plans from the Ship Canal Company.

Chronic dryness, although a virtue in outer walls, is not so when it affects a mouth or an author. It leads in the one case to a thickness of speech, not lessened by subsequent stimulating potations ; in the other case, it probably arises from thickness of skull; and is incurable. _ _

Mouth-breathing is also provocetive, of cold_ on the chest. The outside air is by this method of reddration, conveyed directly to the lungs, and along -with it dust, smoke, and other solid particles, of which the atmosphere of our towns is mostly 'composed. If every man were obliged to consume his own smoke, there would be fewer sweeps and tobacconists than at present. A regulation of this kind would un- doubtedly 'clear' the air somewhat, although the strain on the social system of our large producers would probably be excessive. . When the weather is cold,respiration through the mouth chills the lungs, and frequently causes their congestion, or what some fashionable doctors call "a cold on the chest." Money in the chest is a necessity on such'occasions ere a cure is effected.

div.head: PEOPLE BOUND TO THE STAKE.
div.p: PEOPLE BOUND TO THE STAKE.

The great majority ef people have to work for a livirg with hands or head, or both. Very we:l. To make ou living we must be able to labour so many hours in a day, days in a week, weeks in a year. Very good again. But suppose we each had an enemy who possessed the power to tie us up with a rope when he pleased. To-day he ties only the left arm, to-morrow the right, the next day a leg, and so Once in a' while he ties us to our bed and keeps us there a week. How much would he cost ut in hard cash in a year? and how much would it be worth to us if we could chain him to a rock or hang him with his own rope? Let us have a rough illustration or two. '

A man was working on the Midland Railway as a signalman. We all know what the position is, and have some idea of the labour and responsibility. Well, he kept at it for several years, never missing a day. Be knew his business, nobody better, and nothing went wrong on his section of the, line; bqt by-and-by his enemy began to tie him up'. Somehow he couldn't eat with a relish any more; when he tried be was taken with such a distress it took all the life out of him. Then he would have times when he was so giddy that every- thing went round and round like a whirligig. If this had happened when he had a signal to set, a collision might have come of it ; happily it did not. Other ropes were tied around him ; he had pains in the chest, and sides, his bowels became costive, tongue coated, bad taste in the mouth, heartburn, weakness, .kc. The doc- tors said he would have to give up his situation; but he couldn't. There were the wife and children to be looked out for, and only his earnings to do it with. But finally he broke down altogether, and was laid up for weeks, unconscious part of the time. Then, we may say, he was tied hand and foot. His enemy had him fast, and came nigh killing him. One day, after the doctors had given him up, his mind was clear, and he remem- bered a medicine—half the bottle full—he bad hidden away in a locker in the signal box and forgotten all about it. He sent for it and took a dose. In less than a month he was a well man; the ropes were all cut away. This medicine was Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and his ailment was indigestion and dyspepsia. But whilst he Was ill with it, he might as well—yes bet- ter—have been tied to a stake.

There are lots of (-saes of this sort all over England—all over the world. A few of them we hear of; millions of them we never hear of. Sometimes it is heart disease sometimes rheumatism; sometimes consumption; some- times general debility; sometimes kidney and bladder complaint; sometimes nervous prostration; sometimes liver disorder. That is, the doctors call it by all these hard names, but at bottom it is indigestion and dyspepsia, all these other se-called diseases are just tokens and symptoms of that—neither more nor less. If a man never had any trouble with his stomach he might live for ever, for aught we can tell. Yet how, in Mercy's name, can a man or a woman work with death and corruption inside of the body—with the stomach full of decayingfood, sending poison through the blood to every joint, muscle, and nerve? This is what dyspepsia does. Indigestion is a slow but sure poison, just as taking so many grains of arsenic) every day would be. Here is another case, that of a railway fireman, who writes from Hartford. Hesays "I have been a sufferer from indigestion and dyspepsia for three years ; I tried several doctors, but got worse all the time. At List I went to a chemist and he promised to cure me in a week or two. He sold me three very expensive bottles of medicine, and all the effect I felt from it was the loss of my money. Then I got hold of a bottle of Mother Seigel's Syrup, and was better almost at once. How sorry lam I didn't use it years ago!" We can give this man's name if you care to have it. He didn't want it printed. But he was as good as tied up for a long while. Illness is a strong rope.

Here is one more illustration. Mr. R. B. Hopton, of Long Weston, says: "I am sixty-eight years old. Mother Seigel's Syrup has not quite made me a young man again, but it has cured me of asthma, nervous prostration, and a throat ailment arising from impure blood. I was too ill to labour, yet can now do my work, thanks to that great remedy. You naay publish the fact. The whole complication came first from indiges- tion."
And this is the way people are bound until Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup sets them free.

TWO MONTHS LATER.

" HAYS pity on his weakness, Mark; you are the elder and stronger. You have a wifl of your own. Poor Martin is weak, but he always means well. Take care of him—fight for him. I leave him to you." Every word seemed engraven upon Mark Wool. ford's heart as he sat in the darkened room—words of the sweet, gentle mother lying above stairs—dead— the poor invalid whose tender spirit had seemed F o grieved whenever he spoke harshly towards his younger brother—that handsome, high-spirited, wilful boy, whom his mother had always seemed to worship, while her love for him was placid and calm. And yet there was no jealous feeling in his breast, for as he thought it over he could see how deep and earnest, in spite of its placid flow, had been that mother's love, and he felt thankful that be had kept from her the troubles of the past winter—troubles which flitted through hie mind as he sat in that darkened room.

For how had Martin kept his word? It was with fear and trembling that Mark paid the debt due to Worrell. expecting, as he did, that this would be the signal for other vultures to swoop down. And ac it proved, for one after another he had appli- eations from no less than seven of the snorting brotherhood for various sums, which Martin admitted be owed, and on the strength of his renewed promise these amounts were paid. For a whole, week afterwards Martin was punctual with his duties, old Klopstock shaking his head the while, and then he once more fell. The temptat.on to bet was too strong for him, and three weeks later he was as deeply involved as ever. And Mark Woolford knew it as he sat thinking in that darkened room. Of late years he hod been his mother's counsellor and stay, and her love for his brother had seemed so much stronger because of the way in which she had interposed to screen him when in disgrace. "Yoor Martin—he is so high spirited!" she used to say, and then her imploring look would disarm Mark's resentment, and he would turn away patiently to bear one of his heavy loads. . .

Mark sat there thinking, with his brow wrinkled with sorrow, and his head resting upon his hand. Two days dead—passing away at last in a calm slumber, after years of suffering borne with the patience of a martyr. It seemed so hard to believe that he should never look into her soft, loving epee again—never feel Le gentle pressure of her hand when he returned from tha office of an evening, for now she was really and truly at rest. It was very, very hard to believe, but it was true. 'Poor Martin!" he said, with a sigh. " But I will do my beet." Then he recalled how little his mother bad said respecting Ruth, the orphan child of a dear old friend, who had for years shared their home—poor Ruth, who, after long and patient watching at the in- valid's bedside, had broken down, and was now in turn an invalid. "Another charge for me," be thought. " She said nothing, but she knew me well enough to trust me without a word. Ptor Ruth! I almost envy her the tears that she has shed."

In tho softened twilight of that room a smile seemed lo play about his lips, and his eyes for the moment brightened—the handsome grey eyes, the only good point in his stern, massive countenance, with its thick, dark beard and eyebrows, and broad forehead, which gave him the aspect o 2 a much older man. For Mark Woolford was no handsome youth, but a firm, thoughtful man, some eight years his brother's senior. But at the same time, in that firm thoughtful face there was a look of gentleness and truth— more, there was *peculiar lighting up of his eyes as he eeased for a moment to dwell upon his bereavement, and dreamed on of a fair sweet face with its thick tresses of auburn hair and the deep sad eyes that seemed always to droop and shrink from his searching gaze. Ruth bad always looked up to him with awe. He had been a man grown when she came to them quite a child, and was at once the playmate and companion of his brother. Often and often he had sat and listened to her sweet, rippling laugh as she ran and played with Martin, while a change had always come over her when he approached. At the same time she had always given him a sweet sisterly love, and seemed, like his mother, to lean upon him for help; but he sighed as he thought of the gap that seemed to exist between them, and the lines grew deeper in his forehead as he thought. For it was of his brother now.

Heaven help me !" he said softly, and he rose and walked upstairs to where, in the silent chamber, lay the form of the mother he had loved. He kneeled down for a time, and then row strengthened, bent over the bed, and kissed the cold, white forehead, and remained there gazing at the well- loved face.

"Believe me, I will, dear mother,"nhe raid softly, " Best peacefully in that belief. Come what may, let the call be what it will, your sweet spirit shall pervade all I do. He shall have, poor wilful boy, a brother's care, a man's help and prudence—all that patience and strength can give. Come what may—let the sacrifice lam called upon to make be what it will. For your sake:"

Rash or no it was a great promise to have made— a promise as sacred as the strongest oath; and at that moment, even if he had been able to see outspread before him the tremendous sacrifiues he would be called upon to make, he would not have shrunk from that which he undertook. As he stood there .his overwrought fancy made him we a faint smile play reund to lips of the dead in answer to his own. Then all seam cold and stern once more, sad he slowly left the room to descend and resume his seat in the darkened parlour below. He had not been seated there many minutes before a tall, dark elderly lady mitered the room with a litsle tray, upon which was a lunch tureen of beef tea, a plate of crisp toast, anipt a glass of sherry, the whole of which she placed upon the table by his side. - Hers was not a pleasant face to gam upon, for it wrea tight and hard and yellow. There was a froeen, seared look about it, as if she were fruit that had been left too long upon the tree and hadlecame Soured arid iiirbere;, while the natural moistness had died away; while, to make matters less agreeable, there was a sharp, jerky way pervading everything she did. " Now, Mr. Woolford," she said, ie a harsh tone that, jarred noon hiro " von have had no breakfast; you ate nothing yestirrday, and if you don't have this directly you'll break down." "How is Ruth, Miss Klepstock ?" he saki, eagerly. "I came to bring yJit some food," she replied, shortly," not to talk about !f nth." " Yes ; but tell me. Is she better?" "Ruth only wants rest a little womanly atton• tion, and she will soon he c h." _

He uttered a sigh o!' retia. "Has Martin returned ?" Mize Blopatock tightened her lips and gloat her head. " Apt him to see me as ton as be comes in." Why, bless the man, some plans must be msde for yair Her words, uttered at mach a time, seemed to jar upon him; but he lowiw the speaker well, and what existed beneath that Lard crust, and he bent, him head us if in acquiescence. "Go on, Miss Klopstock," said Mark hoarsely, for the lady had paused only for him to speak. "Well, then, Mark, there is not much to say, but, as an old and dear friend of your poor mother, who held you hi her arms when you were a baby, and I must sal it, Mark, meaning no disrespect to you, for you have grown up a most worthy young man, you were thin ugliest baby I ever saw." Mark smiled faintly, and let his forehead droll °pc° his hand. • "Let me see; what was I saying? Oh, I know, continued Miss Klopstock. "Something must be dona about Ruth." "What can be done?" said Mark, in a low tone. "Well, there are only two courses open, Mark." • " And they are—?" "She must either come and live with me, or I Inur* come and live with her." "But would you forsake your little home and eorne • and live with us?" said Mark, eagerly. „id the "Well, I don't know, Mark Woolford," lady, sharply.' - "for though I maid get cn very well with you and Ruth, as for that boy Martin----" , sure my brother will join with us in trying"" make you a comfortable home, Mire; Klopstock: The lady made a peculiar grimace, and remain' silent for a few moments. div.head: CHORLION CHILD MURDER.
div.p: THE CHORLION CHILD MURDER.

The following memorial has been signed by the jury in the Chorlton child murder trial, and sent to the Home Office :—"We, the undersigned, being the jury who tried Elizabeth Mapp, at the Manchester Assizes, on March 6th, 1890, when she was convicted of the murder of her child and sentenced to death, desire by this memorial to emphasize the strong recommendation to mercy by which our verdict was accompanied, and to express our earnest hope that the death sentence may be commuted, and that in this most sad and painful case the utmost clemency of the Crown may be shown towards this un- fortunate woman."

div.head: RESPITE GRANTED.
div.p: RESPITE GRANTED.

On Thursday morning, Major Preston, the governor of her Majesty's goal at Strangeways, received a comMuni- cation from the Home Secretary respiting the sentence of death passed upon Elizabeth Mapp at the Manchester Assizes, for the murder of her infant child at Chorlton- cum-Hardy. The most wide-spread sympathy and pity had been excited by the prisoner's unfortunate position, as was testified by the numerous petitions in course of preparation and the various suggestions for enforcing the recommendation to mercy which the jury had con- siderately appended to their verdict, and which every- one who became acquainted with the peculiarly painful facts of the case eagerly endorsed.

THE CANADIAN TRAGEDY. VERDICT OF THE JURY. IA cablegram from New York says that the verdict of the coroner's jury at Princetown. Ontario, is that Ben- well came to his death at the hands of Burchall, and they implicated Burchall' s wife as having a guilty knowledge of the crime after its commission. When the inquest was resumed on Saturday morning, Pelley was taken to the grave of the murdered man whosebody was exhumed and identified by Pelley. When in the witness-box at the inquest Pelley told the story as already known as to how they had all come together. Pelley swore that Mrs. Burchall on one occasion spoke to him about a famous' farm at Niagara, explaining that she disliked to . live in the house on a farm, and it was lonely. Burchall fre- quently spoke about his farm and his business in the presence of his wife. Mrs. Burchall was' also present when the arrangements were made by which Burchall and Benwell were to go to the Niagara Falls, for the pur- pose of visiting the farm,and making preparations for the reception.of the party, and on Monday after Burchall and Banwell had left for the farm, she looked in a store at Buffalo at some new wallpaper, with a view of secur- ing some for the house. The witness then identified the clothing found on Benwell's body. Among other docu- Ments found on Burchall'a effe,cts was a letter from Clement, Cheese, and Green, 113, Pill Mall, dated 6th Juno 1889, and addressed to him it Woodstock, inform- ing him that hehad been adjudicated a bankrupt, and had rendered himself liable to criminal proceedings, and to be arrested and brought back to England. What action Burchall took in this matter does not appear. BURCHALL'S CONNECTION WITH LANCASHIRE. Reginald Burchall, the young man arrested in Canada for the murder of Mr. Benwell, is the son of the late Rev. jeseph Burchall, for nearly forty years rector of Church Birk, and for Many years rural dean of Whalley and proctor in convocation, and a member of a well-known and wealthy Lancashire family. When the suspect ad- mitted in court that he was born at Church, Lanca- shire the opinion prevailed in the locality that he must be the son of the late rector. The details as to his age, education, and so on went to confirm the supposition. Young Burchall's life has been a very romantic one. He was born at the rectory at Church, and his father was a man of considerable wealth, being interested in a large brewery, in addition to receiving a good stipend as rector of Church Kirk, one of the oldest churches in the an- cient parish of Whalley. Mr. Burchall was twice mar- ried, and had several children, One is now a clergy- man in the South, and two of the daughters are married to Lancashire clergymen. Reginald Burchall, who is in his twenty-fifth year, left Church on the death of his father, some twelve years ago—he would then be about thirteen—and he was sent to Oxford. As a youth, he was very smart, but fond of life. The fortune left him by his father was soon squandered, and he acquired very loose habits. Last year Burchall left the country to evade his creditors, and told his friends thathewas going toAustralia. It tnrned out that he did not go there, and as his whereabouts could not be ascertained he was de- clared bankrupt. In Church and neighbourhood, the case has caused considerable commotion, and general sympathy is expressed for the family. • STATEMENT BY THE FATHER OF MRS. BURCHALL. In an interview with a representative of the Central News, Mr. David Stephenson, goods station superinten- dent of the London and North-Western Railway, stated that he entirely renudiates the suggestion that his daughter. the wife of 13urchall,was accessory either before or after the crime. He is positive that she had no guilty knowledge after the murder, and was never recognisant of the intentions of her husband. In contradiction of the statements that she.was cnly the pseudo-wife of Burchall, Mr. Stevenson says he has in his possession a copy of her marriage certificate, and he believes that Burchall, or his wife, has the original. He has complete trust in his daughter's innocence, which he believes will be conclu- sively established at the trial. Mr. Stephenson appears almost prostrated. He leaves England in a few days for the scene of the murder. He expresses great apprecia- tion of the sympathetic references to himself in various newspapers. A correspondent, telegraphing from Clifton, Ontario, on Wednesday night, sass that the examination at the Court House of Birchall "for the murder of Mr. Benwell did not begin until nearly six o'clock. Great excitement prevails in the town. Mr. Pickthall themissing English- man, has been heard from. COMMITTAL OF THE ACCUSED. NEW YORK TainisDAY.—The examination of Birchall under charge of murdering Mr. Benwell has concluded, and accused committed to prison to await trial. His wife remained under surveillance for eight days, but will then be liberated unless evidence is brought against her.

BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY.

• MEETING AT WARRINGTON. The annual meeting of the Warrington Auxiliary of this Society was held at the Sankey-st Co- operative Rill, on Monday evening. Mr. John Fairclough presided, and amongst the rather small audience were the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, John Gunnell, John Yonge, J. W. Varley, S. Wilkinson, and Mr. W. Owen, the hon. treasurer. _

MORE SUPPORT WANTED.' The Chairman, in the course of a few opening remarks, said that he regretted that the people of Warrington did not support the Bible Society to the extent they ought; their town was increasing, and so ought the funds of the society to increase. So far as he could see, the real workers of the society were too few. He regretted to say that Mr. John Guest, who had done so much for them for some considerable time, had sent in his resignation as ' collector. The Committee were endeavouring to remedy the small amount of the subscriptions, and to re- organize, and he hoped the result would be a great bene- fit to the society. They wanted willing helpers, and if anyone was anxious to render them assistance they would be very pleased to welcome him or her. THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT, Mr. W. Owen then presented the annual statement of accounts, from which it appeared that the total receipts amounted to £lB4 Bs. 3d., and thp expenditure (including a sum of £lOO given to the parent society) to £ll3 13s. 2d., leaving a cash balance in hand of £7O 15s. Id. Mr. Guest had collected £3O, Mrs. Garnett £l7 9s. 5d., Miss Dutton £8 9s. Bd., Miss Yates £1 18s. Od., and the following collections had been made :—Warrington £2 Us. 9d., Penketh £2 ss. Bd., and Moore £1 14s. 4d. Mr. Owen explained that the Bible Society had a very large stock of Bibles on hand, valued at £7O, and there was owing on account for Bibles to the parent society a large amount, and the nett balance of the society at the pre- sent was estimated at L5l. It should be stated that Mr. J. L. Tunstall kindly audited the accounts each year free of charge. The people of Warrington had never been pressed to increase the amount of their subscrip- tions to the society. He had never been pressed to do so, but he believed that if they were, the subscription would not only be doubled, but in many cases quadrupled. LECTURE BY THE REV. JELINDER E. SIMONS. ' The Rev. J. E. Symons, F.R.G.S., the district secre- tary. then delivered a lecture illustrated by lime-light views, Which was entitled "Round the world with-the" Bible." The lantern had been lent by Mr. F. W. Monks, and it was worked by Messrs. Alfred C4rney and E. Wallington. A large number of views were thrown on the screen, and a graphic description of each was given by the lecturer. Views were shown of Turkey, Japan, India, Canada, and other lands, and in concluding, Mr. Symons said he had only touched upon the fringe of the work of the society. He thanked the audience very much for the kind attention they had paid to his observations, and he hoped the effect of the meeting would be to stir up their hearts so that they would put forth increased efforts on behalf of the society. ELECTION OF OFFICERS, &C. During the evening, the Rev. J. Symons moved "That the treasurer's statement be printed for the use of the subscribers and that the following gentlemen be the officers and Committee of the auxiliary for the ensuing year :—President," Lord Winmarleigh •' vice-presidents, sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart, M.P., and Mr. John Crosfield, J.P. • treasurer, Mr. William Owen, F.R.1.8.A., secretaries, the Rev. E. C. E. earleton, the Rev. John Yonge, and Mr. P. Silcock ; Committee, Messrs. William Barlow, E. J. Guest, 8.A., J.P., John Guest, R. Garnett, J.P., Z. Armitage, J.P., R. A. Naylor, J. Fairclough, LP., J. R. Buckton, H. Horden, and G. White, and the local clergy and ministers." The Rev. John Gunnell seconded the motion, which was carribd:—The Rev. S. Wilkinson, in proposing a :vote of thanks to Mr. Fairclough for presiding over the meeting, said that that gentleman had for many years been a warm supporter of the society. —the Rev. John ' Yon„ve seconded the motion, and said he hoped that what Mr. Fairclough had told them that night would have the effect of making them take A greater interest 1 lin the Bible Society. That a town of the size of War- ringtonovhich contained so many churches and chapels, Should only produce the paltry and insignificant sum of £34 to the funds of such an excellent society was to him a great surprise. Why should ladies and gentlemen be required to be "pressed" to contribute to such a society ? If they believed in the glorious Book, they would not want pressing, but would contribute as libe- rally as their means would allow. He hoped that the efforts of the ladies would be crowned with success, and that instead of receiving £34 every year, that that amount would be doubled or even quadrupled.—The motion was heartily agreed to, and the Chairman having briefly acknowledged the compliment, the Benediction was pronounced and the nroceedings terminated.

THE ATTEMPTED MURDER QF JUDGE
BRISTOWE.

• • -- Edward Wilhelm Ernest Arnemann, a German dentist was found guilty at Nottingham, on Saturday, of attempting to murder Judge 13ristowe, on November 19, last. The prisoner was nonsuited by the judge in a county court suit on the day named, and, following the judge to the railway station, shot him with a revolver, and wounded him so seriously that his life was for a time in danger. The prisoner was sentenced to 20 years' penal servitude.
TWO HUNDRED SOLDIERS MASSACRED

div.head: FEMALE GEiTEAL KILLED.
div.p: A FEMALE GEiTEAL KILLED.

Advices from Konoton state that the King of Dahomey has retired with his Amazons to Lano, after having re- mained four days in Godomeywithoutmusteringcourage to attack the French posts. Altogether the Dahomeyans have lost about a thousand men since the opening of the campaign, and the general of the Amazons, a woman, has been killed. The six Frenchmen who were taken prisoners have been brought back to Whydah. A SLEEP-WALKING ACTRESS.

A policeman on duty in Broadway, New York, on Monday night. met a ghostly-looking figure, and was so frightened at the apparation that he took to His heels. A brother officer, who had more courage, arrested the sup- posed spectre, and discovered it to be flesh and blood. It was Miss May Case, one of the chorus girls of the Casino Theatre, fast asleep, with nothing on but her chemise. The policeman hastily wrapped his overcoat around her and carried her in his arms to the neighbour- ing police station, where she awakened and went into a fit of hysterics.

div.head: FRIGHTFUL CRIME IN CANADA.
div.p: FRIGHTFUL CRIME IN CANADA.

A FAMILY MURDERED. The American newspapers to hand by mail bring par- ticulars of a fiendish crime committed by a young farmer, named Rudolph Dubois, at St. Albans, a village midway between Montreal and Quebec. Dubois, although a hard-working man, had an ungovernable temper, and was madly but unjustly jealous of his wife, a young and remarkably handsome woman. The family consisted of Dubois, his wife, his wife's mother (Mrs. Thebault), and two children, Joseph, aged four, and George aged four months. Nothing is known of the im- mediate dispute which• led to the tragedy, which was discovered on a Sunday morning by some neighbours who, failing to obtain admission, forced open the door of the house. The place resembled a slaughter-house. Mrs. Dubois, her mother, and the children were all found murdered, and their bodies had been mutilated. Search parties were at once organised, and Dubois was tracked to a wood and there arrested, after a desperate struggle. Au attempt was made to lynch him, but he was safely lodged in gaol.

div.head: DEATH SENTENCE FOR WIFE MURDER
div.p: DEATH SENTENCE FOR WIFE MURDER

Thomas Neal, aged 88 years, blacksmith, was indicted at the Central Criminal Court, London, on Saturday, for the wilful murder.of his wife, Theresa Neal, by cutting her throat. The prisoner hail no counsel, but at the re- quest of the court Mr. Geoghegan defended him. The deceased woman was only 24 years of age, and she was married to the Prisoner in the year 1883, at which time she was only 18 years of age. The marriage was a very unhappy one. At the time of the murder they occupied a lodging in St. Peter's-st., Islington. On the morning of the 28th of JanuaJanuarythe sounds of a violent struggle were heard in the prisoner's room, and the wife appeared to have exclaimed. "Oh, Bill, don't kill me: I love you with all my heart." Very shortly after this the woman was found in the street with a terrible wound in the throat. She was removed to the hospital, where she died soon afterwards. The jury found the prisoner guilty, and he was sentenced to death.

The Roman Catholic Bishop of Raphoe has forwarded to the Irish Tenants' Defence Fund the sum of £1,017 es. 10d., as the contribution of the parishes of Donegal in- cluded in the see of Raphoe. A NEW TEMPERANCE CRUSADE. The "Freeman's Journal" says:—" At a Synodic meeting of the Archbishop and Suffragan Bishops of the Province of Dublin, on Friday, arrangements were made for the organization of an effective temperance move- ment throughout the diocese of Dublin and the suffragan dioceses of Kildare and Leighton Ferns and Ossory. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A DOCTOR. At Cappawhite, Tipperary, on Saturday, Dr. Robert A. Webb, a medico: practitioner, was charged before a special court with having with a razor cut the throat of Patrick Kelly, a constable of the Royal Irish Constabul- ary. It appeared that Kelly and a publican went to Dr. Webb's house, the former to have a tooth extracted or stopped, and while there the parties had drink. At Con- stable Kelly's request Dr. Webb left this house and went up the village to see if the police were on patrol. This was about 9.30 p.m. On coming back the doctor, find- ing serious occasion to. complain of Kelly's conduct, knocked him out of the room, and then, seizing a razor, inflicted a terrible gash in the constable's neck. The doctor, however, immediately,.stitched up the wound, but not before life was nearly extinct. The defendant was remanded on bail. LADY GUARDIANS., ASSERTING THEMSELVES, I The Warrington Board of Guardians, at their meeting, on Wednesday, were asked to supply some unusual information. The following letter was read from Mr. Dickson, Clerk to the Ormskirk Union. " Will you oblige our Guardians by answering the questions annexed at your earliest convenience? I I feel I ought to offer some sort of apology for the nature of the questions, as they are rather out of the ordinary, but I may just state that we have four lady Guardians on our Board." The first two questions referred to the number of children and officers at Padgate schools, and the next was" Do the girls wear drawers ?"After that came the query " Do•you supply children with tooth brushes ?" and "Have you any lady. Guardians on your Board? If so, how many ?" The CLErac (Mr. J. C. Sutton) : I suppose we may as well tell them (laughter). The CHAIRMAN :01 course—if you can (more laughter). The subject was not pursued further.
DOUBLE EXECUTION AT WORCESTER.

Joseph Boswell, twenty-nine, and Samuel Boswell, thirty-nine, gardeners, were executed at Worcester Gaol on Tuesday morning for the murder of Frank Stephen, a gamekeeper employed by the Due d'Aumale,at Evesham. Alfred Hill, another gardener, was also sentenced to deaths but was on Tuesday reprieved. The jury at the trial strongly recommended the men to the clemency of the Crown, but only in the case of Hill were there found extenuating circumstances sufficient to warrant the interposition of the Home Secretary. The culprits were visited by their relations for the last time on Saturday, when there was a painful interview. Both men were married and had families. They appeared very feeble, and had to be assisted to the gallows, Samuel Boswell almost fainting. Death was instantaneous. • Another account says that the men were placed on the drop. They moaned piteously, and in loud voices made responses to the reading of the Burial Service. Then Joseph said, "Oh, my dear wife; "and Samuel rejoined, "Yes, and my dear children." Joseph said, "Goodbye, Sam ; "and Sam answered, "God bless you, boy. Oh, dear, dear." Samuel exclaimed just before the drop fell, "I hope everybody will do well. Goodbye." A great crowd awaited the hoisting of the black flag outside the gaol, but made no demonstration. The chaplain stated that both the wretched men died penitent. They were not informed down to the moment of the formation of the procession that their companion Hill had been re- prieved.

div.head: LOVER'S TRAGEDY.
div.p: A LOVER'S TRAGEDY.

A young man named George Arthur, a clerk in the employ of Messrs. G. and J. Burns, at Belfast, shot his sweetheart, Nora Paterson, on Wednesday, at a place known as Lovvry's Plantation, Cave Hill. He afterwards shot himself. The girl died immediately, having received three bullets in her forehead, but Arthur lingered, and was found by a workman, who reported the matter to the police. The wounded man was taken to the Royal Hospital, where he died five minutes after admission. From a letter found in his pocket, it appears that the tragedy had been mutually agreed on. Both the deceased were about 26 years of age. It is , said that the crime was the outcome of circumstances which prevented the deceased from marrying. A packet of cartridges and a revolver were foun3 at the scene of the murder. A coroner's jury sitting at Ligoniel, near Belfast, on Thurs- day, found that Nora Patterson was killed by her lover, George Arthur. ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.

Sir George Elliot M.P., (Conservative) for the Mon- mouth District, is stated in a telegram from Cardiff to have placed his resignation in the hands of the Govern- ment whip. The rumour was current throughout South Wales yesterday. Mr. Cunningham Graham has definitely declined to again contest Lanarkshire, on account of want of funds. At a meeting in Glasgow, on Tuesday night a motion thanking him for his services met with Bowie opposition, but was eventually carried. AYR Buns.—A new writ for the Ayr Burghs was ordered in the House of Commons im Wednesday. The nominations will be made on the 20th and the polling will take place on the 25th inst. Mr. John Sinclair, after resigning his seat for the Ayr Burghs, telegraphed to Mr. Edmund Rautledge, the Liberal candidate, wishing him every possible success. Mr. Routledge has been very heartily received at the meetings he has addressed, and obtained votes of confidence. His opponent, Mr. Somer. vill, has also commenced his campaign. The writ for the Ayr Burghs election was received by Sheriff Brand on Thursday morning, and he had con- firmed the dates provisionally fixed on Wednesday, namely, the 20th for the nomination, and the 25th inst. for the polling. The result will be declared on the 26th. STom—Viscount Cranborne, Sir Henry Havelock- Allan, and Mr. Kenrick, members of Parliament, attend- ed a crowded meeting in Longton Town Hall on Wednes- day night, in support of the Unionist "candidate. The proceedings were of the most uproarious description, and the speakers failed to obtain a hearing. A vote of confidence in Mr. Allen was lost. THE STAMFORD ELECTION. The votes were counted at Bourne on Saturday morn- ing, the result being declared as follows : Mr. H. J. A TRAIN OFF THE LINE ON THE FORTH BRIDOE.—A severe gale raged in Edinburgh and district on Monday night and Tuesday morning. While a goods train was crossing the Forth Bridge, the wind blew a bale of cotton off a wagon • the result was that several wagons left the metals, and that for some time traffic had to be conducted by a single line. A portion of the new electrical exhibition buildings was blown down in Edinburgh during the night. Some further correspondence has passed between Mr. Gladstone and Professor Tyndall on the subject of the latter's interpretation of some of the ex-Premier's utter- ances with regard to the Irish question. div.head: EXECUTION AT NEWCASTLE.
div.p: EXECUTION AT NEWCASTLE.

William Row, aged 41 years, shoemaker, was executed on Wednesday morning, in Newcastle Jail, for the murder of Lilian Wilson, a woman with whom he lived, about two months ago. When told on Tuesday that the law must take its course, the culprit simply said he thought the strong recommendation to mercy by the jury might have brought a reprieve, but, as it could not be helped, he was ready to meet his fate. Before being led out of his cell, he said that he believed he could walk well to the scaffold, and the only thing he was afraid about was that he would not be able to stand upright on the drop, as he, being club-footed, never could stand steady with both feet together. He walked pinioned, but had to be steadied on the scaffold. The unfortunate man was penitent, and to the chaplain ascribed his crime to sudden and jealous frenzy.
_ WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs. J. Houghton, Heaton, Davies Hood- Wright, Dobson, Aukland, Kilshaw, Smith, Ratcliffe, Wright, Clarke, J. Houghton, Dignum, T. Jones, Blackhurst, D. Jones, A. Jolley, Mather, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, W. gill, Humphreys; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (Workhouse master), and H. M. Mines (superinten- dent of Padgate Schools). THE Bona Commix-rim—The House Committee recommended that the tender of Mr. Fletcher, of Messrs. Fletcher and Lee, for the supply of 30 quilts be accepted; also that the tender of Mr. William Rose and Co. for a fire hose for the Workhouse be accepted, the question as to the supply of a fire escape to be deferred to next meeting.—The minutes were adopted. Scnom, FEES.—The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 67 cases, 59 of which were old. The Queen with Princess Beatrice and royal suite, left Windsor 'for London, on Thursday, and took up their residence at Buckingham Palace until Saturday. At Brighton on Thursday morning the wife of a rail- way workman, named Feist, cnt the throat of her infant son and then her own. Her husband found them dead in bed when he came home to breakfast. The woman had been in a depressed state of mind, but had pot shown any symptoms of a suicidal character. SUICIDE OF A SCHOOLBOT.—A boy name West, aged 12 years, committed suicide at Great Malvern, on Monday. He several times threatened during the last few days to drown himself. His body was found on Monday in a pond. On the bank was a piece of paper, on which he had written, "Oh, Lord, give me a new heart and Thy Holy Spirit; pardon all my sins, for Christ's sake, Amen." The bank rate of discount was reduced on Thursday from q to 4 per cent. It is understood that the Prince of Wales will be Lord Sefton's guest at Croxeth during the approaching Liver- pool races. Judge Ingham, referring on Wednesday at Barrow County Court to the irregular way in which defendants liable for instalments paid into court, said there was no such thing as imprisonment for debt. He only com- mitted a man to gaol when he knew he had the money and would not pay.
