isi Tux debate in the House of 6/011 sßapeankdsolpohut. mons on the report of the raril,ose Commission was brought to a 0 on Tuesday night. The discussion has was expected, to be most damaging to the ment. A division was taken, on Monday niglrl,t)toed Mr. GLADSTONE'S amendment which ell' sympathy with Mr. PARNELL in having be'ert- justly subjected to foul and slanderous oln'11:0 The amendment was defeated; but the mai°7l;; for the Government was 71 only. On Tnesc—jf Hight when the debate terminated the inai°l4,t',,o the Government was reduced to 62. There been - been abundant signs that the Tories are conaci°ao of doing a mean and shabby thing in refusing tc' two justice to Mr. PARNELL ; but, with one or to, memorable exceptions, they have not as they would have liked, lest their defoor7a should bring . about a dissolution. ilfr. RANDOLPH CHURCHILL did not support ea GLADSTONE'S amendment; but he sPoke's-rict Tuesday evening, on the main resolution ; to. delivered a most powerful speech against be course taken by the Government. It Yin' said that his lordship is a disappointed . and that he is paying off an old score in Atte,'" ing his former colleagues; but it is due to hira„t° state that he has all along disapproved of appointment of the Commission. Further, went the length, as he made known in the Co of his speech, of bringing his views before"; Government by means of a written doown They rejected his advice: they proceeded to dig pit for Mr. PARNELL, !tad they have fallen int°oo themselves. Lord R. CHURCHILL'S speed', .00 Tuesday, treated of the unconstitutional actil of "the constitutional party," and he °teal/La proved his case against the appointment !" Commission. Commencing he said : I lay down the theory that, where the Govel; ment hold there isa prima facie case against pot of incriminated on criminal charges, it is the chltY;_a. the Executive Government to proceed by a crinatT; prosecution in the ordinary manner. But if. on _„, other hand, there was in the opinion of the Govet::, ment, a prima facie ease to justify proceedin7,3.,"!.g. prosecution against the. parties I say a fortiori LIT[O, Mist have been a prim, facie case to ustify Government in asking the House to constitute.ol extraordinary tribunal. If there walrio a facie case for a prosecution, there 'coul'i es- prima facie case to justify Parliament in the or tion of an extraordinary tribunal. her for There can be no qmstion that tile Tern-- d it South Paddington is right i theory, an or puts the case against the GovernMent in a n a n__ shell. The first blunder was the aivintment c'tibe Commission ; and the second was in giving Commission the combined funetions of p&p an'

jury. 9 It What (asked Lord landolph), does that mean means this—that they decided to place P°lit.'ll opponents on their tnal on a. criminal charge W. out giving to those political opponents the Prc'tneeb tion which a jury was eu_pposcd to give. I at tr enormous importance—l cannot help attachl 'enormous importance—to this twitter; the in 161 seiduneer 1.0 acOiget Ntit: I Pr, tf.to

these concerns a British Government is dealing with political opponents. Because the House will see— both sides must see--that what one Government may lawfully do in dealing with political oppon- pe,s another Government may do with equal legal- ity. 'What was the third step ? The third step was, 'laving compelled these individuals—these political opponents—to stand their trial on a criminal Charge, the Executive of the day proceeded them- selves to nominate the members of the tribunal. The points made by his Lordship were well sus- tained; and they were not answered, for the simple reason that they are unanswerable. Con- trasting the way in which the "Times" and the Irish members were being treated, he asked : What do we do if we adopt the report and make it our Own? Do we condemn certain persons of certain charges, and do we acquit other parties con- cerned in this matter? Do we condemn all the Parties who have been found guilty of, to use a very mild expression, misdemeanour? It is quite true that We condemn the Irish members on certain charges and certain acts ; but do we condemn the " Times " newspaper ? The "Times " newspaper, Which has been found to be guilty of an atrocious libel against members of this [louse? Not a word is there in the report, or in your motion, condemning a convicted delinquent, who is certainly in this . Matter as important as the Irish members. Do you, ean you, call that dealing out absolute justice? if the Government insist on this motion, if they corn- Pal their majority to assent to it—then I also insist 11P0n my right, as a member of this House, to record MY vote in favour of the condemnation, not only of the Irish party hut of the " Times " newspaper, found guilty of an atrocious libel upon members of this House, and of a slander unexampled and with- foundation. (Loud cheers.) But the Government have thought otherwise; they have chosen to row in the same boat as the

Times ;" and they dare not condemn the " Times " at they should condemn themselves. The Times " , has got and is still getting its punishment; the turn of the Government has to come with the general Election.

Counin So Seen after the Llanntoh Mining Disasters. catastrophe, the news of another great colliery disaster in South \Vales is in the highest degree appalling. The scene of the calamity of Monday last is the Morfa Colliery, near Port Talbot, Mid-Glamorgan. It is stated, as is usually stated in these cases, that every precaution was taken to ensure the safety of the mine. If this be so, it would seem that frequent explosions in connection with coal-getting arO to be accepted as in the ordinary course of things. But we cannot bring ourselves to accept such a theory; for the careful inquiry which always fellows the terrible loss of life in these cases, ilanally reveals a weak point, regard to which Might have prevented the disaster. The Morf a tame has been worked for forty years, and safety lamps were used. It was regarded as 4 . safe mine, and yet we learn that the ruiners were uneasy a week before the explosion in consequence of the strange sounds they heard whilst they were at work. A special examination *as made, and the conclusion come to was that there was no cause for alarm. The explosion on Monday is an appalling contradiction to the state- Ment that the strange sounds meant nothing. They were in the nature of a warning, and it is a thousand pities that more regard could not have been paid to the warning. We do not say that th, examination must have been a careless one; out, taking into account the frequency of these disasters, we do say that more requires to be done than is done to ensure the safety of those whose hard lot it is to pass" a sunless life in the unwhole- some mine."

We are told that "The Morf a" makes the forty- ' eighth explosion in the South Wales coal fields in fc4ty-four years, the total number of lives lost being nearly 2,200 apart from the present disas- t°r." This is surely sufficient to give us pause. It roust be remembered that the collier is like the Bailor in the readiness with which he goes to his task and braves the dangers which beset him. Het ia hardy and courageous, and too willing, perhaps, to incur risk ; but that is no reason why those who legislate on his behalf should not, if need be, pro- tect him even against himself. A collier, who was gnostioned after the Llanerch explosion on the Preference which was shown for the use of naked llghts, explained that there was constant danger c* fatal accident from falls from the roof, aud the naked light enabled the miner so to see the condi- ticsn of the roof. It would appear therefore that °lle thing that is urgently needed is more light. The miner must have a light on the spot where he 114 Working, and he is surely entitled to be furnished Vith sufficent light to enable him to see when he tin danger of being buried by a fall from the roof. , i:bere are difficulties, doubtless, in the way of hghting workings, and extra lamps means extra coat; but what of that if it adds to the safety of the tens of thousands of men who at present take their . in their hands when they go down each day 440 the bowels of the earth? It has for a genera- on been dinned into our ears that further restric- 'nns upon mining operations would do no good, hlle inflicting heavy costs upon colliery proprie- ,7B ; but we now know from undeniable experience ;nat these restrictions have been the means, nY reducing the number of accidents, of saving thousands of lives. What is required is that there allould be further legislation, so that the miner tnaY have all the protection that the law can give; tilt" 80, too, that it shall not have to be said during ige next forty years that there have been over ZrtY explosions in the coal districts of South "ales.

Tan uncertainty which prevails as Siiiiirl;',lCag nal to what is to be done, at Latchford, in the way of providing bridges 47°88 the Ship Canal is very unsatisfactory. As ;:ue Act of 1885 stands, the Ship Canal Company ZaN'e undertaken to provide three swing bridges -o_ll this district—one at Acker's-lane, another at Ppenhall-road, and the third at Knutsford- ad. We have all along been of opinion that it is the interests of the inhabitants to hold the 'lnPariy to this engagement, for we do not see N°ll3' the public should be put to inconvenience for ,ever in order to save something to-day in the alting of the Canal. What the Company wish to m° is to avoid being put to the cost of making one of the three swing bridges. There have been sq ndry consultations and meetings; and what was litrlderstood to be a final arrangement was the accep- :nee of a proposal to get rid of one of the bridges Placing a swing bridge between Knutsford-road Chappenhall-road, the bridge thus both roads. By way of compensation for the loss "e swing bridge, it was settled that there Should Swing a high level foot-bridge across the canal t a point which would give access to the new Istation to be erected at Latchford. But these 71.11-laid plans are all awry; for the Daresbury Were IgliwaY Board, as the road authority, ~ ~aged, at a special meeting, on Moo- tut• Y' in considering a proposal to substi- would a high level vbhicular bridge. This enable people, though at some incon- jrnence, to cross the canal at any time; but the 13,4 c", PanY Bay—" If you want a liigh level vehicular "'uge, you must sacrifice the swing bridge at -21eker.8-141)e ; for we will not make both." It be-
serving

comes again a question of cost; and as to this we hold that the interests of the inhabitants of Latchford and of Warrington must not be sacri- ficed in order that the Ship Canal Company may effect a saving on the making of bridges. Before any final decision is come to, there should be another meeting of the inhabitants of Latchford. They have twice been consulted, and they should be consulted again if new plans are to be sub- mitted. The Corporation of Warrington are given, under the Bill, a voice in the matter, and it will be their duty to exercise that voice if anything should be proposed which would make access to the town less easy than it has hitherto been. We look to the Ship Canal becoming a help and not a hindrance to Warrington.

div.head: "TOUCH. AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH. AND GO."

The Governmmit have turned deaf cars to the cry for better treatment of our Volunteers, and on Thursday night they were "wakened up." They were defeated on a motion on the subject, the majority against them being 33. "Serve 'em right."

A poll is about to be taken in "Tit-hits," the result of which will be of some interest. The ques- tion which is put in this week's issue is, " Have you confidence in the Government ?" The poll closes on the 19th March ; and we venture to pre- dict that, as the readers of " Tit-bits are of the average type of Englishmen, the majority of the answers will be" No."

Sir Charles Dilke has been silent for some time, but he has not been drifting. He is still an ad- vanced Liberal. He spoke a hopeful word at Glasgow, on Tuesday, remarking that a time of more equal distribution of wealth was at hand, and that he looliad forward to " a period when the worker would be King in great Britain as he was already King in ustralia

--- There have been no less than three fatal acci- dents on the Ship Canal Works during the past week. As many as 50 lives were lost in the construction of the Forth Bridge, and it would seem as if as many will be lost in the making of the Ship Canal. Great indeed are the achieve- ments a the ago, and great ie the price paid for them,

--- Daniel Crasby made his 66th appearance at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday. He was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and promised, as usual, that he would take the pledge. Reminded of the way in which he had previously broken it, he said—" I will filful ' my promise this time." But the Bench thought he would be more likely to fill-full "a foaming mug ; and accordingly sent him to gaol for a month, with hard labour.

The plain tnglish of the correspondence between Professor Tyndall and Mr. Gladstone is that the Professor has " made a fool of himself." He has shown in his railing the spirit of a fish-wife. Much learning must have made him mad. In his reply, Mr. Gladstone takes it easy. He says : It seems to give you pleasure and it causes me no pain." It is as the navvy said when his wife began to beat him—" It pleases she, and don't hurt me."

Three Newton boys have been playing brutal pranks with sheep—such as tying up the mouth of one, and tying three together by the hind legs. The result was that five of the animals were more or less injured. A fine of ss. and costs was inflicted in each case, the magistrates expressing their re- gret that they had not the power to give a good birching. But this is a defect which the parents might remedy. If they spare the rod, they may spoil the children.

The rung woman who was charged with shoot- ing Major Isaacs, M.P. for Walworth,was acquitted on Tuesday. She was given the benefit of a doubt as to whether the shooting was wilful. The inci- dont is a revelation as to the character of the Major; and, following on the case of:Colonel Hughes-Hallett, it is another stain upon the re- putation of Tory M.P.s. Ah ! if we only knew all I "Give me an ounce of civet, good apothecary, to sweeten my imagination !"

G. H. Pillinger, the Warrington man who attempted to poison himself near Wrexham, on Saturday, is according to his own written confes- sion " a scamp and a vaggerboon." It turns out that, unlike many others, his confession is a true one. He has ill-treated his wife so much and so often that it would, perhaps, have been all the better if he had taken a little more laudanum. As it is, he is alive, and he will soon be kicking—if he is to keep up his reputation as "a scamp and a vaggerboon."

Mr. Richard Power is the chief Whip of the Irish Parliamentary party; and he is allied with those who have been gibbeted by the Judges." According to the Tory way of looking at things, Mr. Power must be "a vile conspirator," "a double-dyed traitor and yet this monster of iniquity" was amongst the select few who dined with the Prince of Wales on Saturday. Ha !Ha !! But this must be seen to. Perish the Prince! Perish England I rather than let "such things be, and overcome us like a summer cloud "

Mr. Labouchere has been holding Mr. Houston of Pigott fame up to ridicule in a parody in "Truth," and Mr. Houston has sent a lawyer's letter demanding an apology. Mr. Labouchere has not yet apologised, and it is suggested that if apologies are to he the order of the day, M. Houston might show the way by apologising to Mr. Parnell.

Poor, wretched, despicable Pigott! He seems to have written everybody in the hope that he might bleed them as he bled the over-kind late W. E. Forster. It transpires that he wrote Lord Salis- bury, asking for an interview; but it does not transpire why his lordship declined to accord him one. Can it be that the Prime Minister made inquiries, and found, as Sir William Harcourt expressed it, that Pigott was not fit to be touched with a forty-foot pole?

Lord Randolph Churchill rang the changes on Pigott with some effect in his speech in the House of Commons, on Tuesday evening. He said "Nemesis has overtaken the Government. What is the result of its upheaval of the British Consti- tution? What has been the one result? Pigott. (Loud Opposition cheers.) What has been the re- sult of this mountainous parturition? A thing, a reptile, a monster—Pigott. (Loud cheers.) What has been the result of this deliverance? With all your skill and all your Parliamentary instruments —a ghastly, bloody, rotten Pigott"! Pigott r! Pigott! U (Laughter and cheers). It need hardly be said that Lord Randolph was in a state of high tension during the delivery of his important speech on Tuesday evening. In the course of its delivery he axpressed a wish for a drink of water. The "Star" says that "several Tory members refused in succession to do this simple act of natural kindness." And this from "the party of gentlemen !" Shame on them Mr. Bauman was more considerate, and finally fetched a glass of water, amid the cheers of the Opposi- tion.

Lord Randolph hit the Government so hard that it put Mr. Jennings, who should have moved an amendment, into something like a funk. He left it to Mr. Caine to move the amendment which stood in his name, but it is only fair to say of the Tory member for Stockport that he, too, spoke out. Referring to " Parnellism and Crime" he said : "No device was left untried to induce the public to believe that Mr. Parnell and some of his collea- gues were murderers and assassins. The net was constructed so widely that there seemed no possibi- lity of escape, and he declared that even now it was to him a marvel that they had escaped. Opposi- tion cheers.) Never was a man placed in greater jeopardy, and however much they might object to his policy, he thought they must feel sympathy with him in his escape from such diabolical charges. (Opposition cheers.)

POOR RATES AT RUNCORN. Mr. W. Sutton, assistant overseer, Runcorn, summoned 59 persons to the Police Court, on Monday, for non-pay- ment of the poor rate. 53 of the cases were settled out of Court ; and the magistrates dealt with the remaining number of cases in the usual manner.

WIDNES WHITS ROSS Cracts'r CLUB. In connection with this Club a concert W 0,5 Pfeil in the Baths Assembly Room, on Thursday evening and there was a fair attendance. A capital programme of songs, &c., was gone through by Messrs. W. Smith, H. Pil- grim, W. A. Edwards, T. Fox, J. Pennington, G. Kiddie, A. Shingler, T. Wailing, W. Baldwin, P. Kenyon, J. Nickson, and T. Lockett. Mr. Howell Donne was the accompanist. The proceeds are to be devoted towards erecting a pavilion on the cricket ground.

- - CANTATA AT WIDNES. The sacred cantata " Belshazzat's Feast" was rendered in the Drill Hall, Widnes, on Thursday evening, by a choir of 50 voices under the conductorship of Mr. J. Platt. There was a good attendance. Major Wareing read the narrative, and the principal vocalists were Miss Poulson, soprano; Mrs. Bevan, contralto ; Mr. T. Bevan, tenor ; Mr. W. Thomas, tenor; Mr. J. Williams, baritone; and Mr. J. R. Lea, bass. Mr. J. T. Jones played the accompaniments on the harmonium. The cantata was gone through in capital style, and the audience frequently manifested their approval. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at an hours' nottce.—J. & W. Dutton, Sankey-street. ALARMING FIRE AT RUNCORN. About ten o'clock on Thursday night, the inhabitants of Runcorn were startled by the blowing of the whistle at the works of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Co., and hundreds were quickly on the spot prepared to see the works in flames. Fortunately the cause of the alarm was not the works, but a shippon belonging to Mr. Reuben Peacock, which had become ignited through a patent heating apparatus. The cows were quickly and safely removed, and in less than ten minutes a number of men had extinguished the fire by means of buckets of water, and the damage done is not very great.

• TRH RABIES ORDER AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Clough, butcher, Church-st., was summoned for allowing his dog to be at large, insecurely muzzled. P.C. Wood- row said the defendant's dog and a dog belonging to Mr. Blythe were fighting. Both the animals were muzzled; but the defendant's dcg bit off the ear of Blythe's dog. The defendant had been warned that his dog was not securely muzzled.—The defendant said the small bit of leather across the front of the muzzle was cut through, but he had had it repaired.—A fine of' Is. and costs 9s. 6d. was imposed .—Thomas Faulkner was summoned for hav- ing his dog at large. The wife appeared and said her hus- band was stillman at the Old Quay works and could npt attend the Court. Mr. Thomas: He ought to be here. Adjourned for a week. div.head: CRUELTY TO A PONY AT RTYNCORE.
div.p: CRUELTY TO A PONY AT RTYNCORE.

At Runcorn Police Court on Monday, William Rawlin- son, a greengrocer, was summoned for cruelly ill-treating a pony by working it while in an unfit state. Inspector Wilson R.S.P.C.A. of Altrincham, deposed that on the 27th February he was in Runcorn, and in Lord-st. he saw the defendant in charge of a pony drawing a cart laden with vegetables. The animal was exceedingly lame on the fore leg, the knee being much swollen and inflamed, and was in very great pain and unfit for work. —P.S. Gosling said the pony had been lame ever since the defendant had it, and was unfit for work.—The de- fendant said he had called in Mr. Bate the veterinary surgeon, who said the horse was quite fit to work.—The case was adjourned until the close of the Court, so that Mr. Bate could attend and giveevidence. He, however, was not to be found and the defendant was fined 10s. and costs Us. 6d. A BREWERS' BATTLE AT RUNCORN. Yesterday afternoon a sale of property was held at South Bank Hotel, Runcorn, by Mr. T. Sutton, ot War- rington, and there was a very large attendance. The chief interest centred in the disposal of the South Bank Hotel, Lord-st., and of the Queen's Head Hotel, Water- loo-road. For the latter place, which is a corner house ef only medium size, the competition was very keen be- tween the representatives of two great firms of brewers —Messrs. A. B. Walker and Co., and Messrs. Whitley, Greenall, and Co., of Wilderspool Brewery. The bidding commenced at £l,OOO, and advanced by hundreds to £l,BOO, when the bids dropped to £5O. and finally to £5. the property being eventually knocked down to Messrs. Walker for £2,570. The battle between the brewers caused considerable CLEcitement. There was apparently no great desire to possess South Bank Hotel, which, after two bids, was withdrawn at £3,100, the re- :serve amount being stated. 721PRELL AS RE-COVERED at an hours' notice.—J. Er. W. Dutton, Sankey-street. I BURLARY AT SUTTON WEAVER. Before Mr. James Handley at Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, William Twist, who has been twice con- victed, was charged with having on the 11th inst. burglariously entered Park Farm, Sutton, occupied by Alfred Lomas, with intent to steal. The li.iuse was properly secured on the night of the 10th inst. and at twenty minutes to five next morning Peter Lomas, father of the prosecutor, went downstairs into the kitchen, when he found the prisoner standing with his shoes off. 'The prisoner said lie had got through the window and wanted something to eat. Lomas took the key out of the kitchen door and placed it in his pocket, and the prisoner rushed into the lobby, and held the door of the kitchen so that he could not leave the place. He shouted to his son, who came to his aid and the pri- soner was secured. Lie prisoaer pleaded hard for his liberty, and offered to give a watch he had in his pos- session, but he was subsequently given into the custody of P.C. Costello, to whom on the way to the police station he also offered his watch in return for his release. The prisoner had entered the farm by removing a pane of glass from the window, but he had been disturbed before he could steal anything. The prisoner was committed to Chester A:Azes for trial. The watch, found in the prisoner's possession had been identified as stolen from Bedford Leigh.

Mac Kinder, M.A. The subject was the " Gulf Stream," which the lecturer dealt with in his usual lucid and eloquent style, and he was aided in his descriptions by the oxy-hydrogen 'Mee light, manipu- lated by Mr. H. IMPUDENT THEFT AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, W. Rowlings was charged with stealing a pair of trousers and a tiuernsey from the shop of Arnold Unsworth, High-st. On the previous day the prisoner entered the shop under the influence of drink for the purpose of talking to the shop boy, James Higgins. When he left the place he was seen to conceal the articles under his coat. lie was after- wards apprehended by Inspector Bowyer.—The prisoner said he was drunk and did not remember anything about the robbery. He was lined 31s. or go to gaol for 14 days. BASINETTES, new designs.--Garland, Ironmonger, War- rington.—A drt.

FCNERAL OF THE LATE MR. JOHN ANDERSON AT WIDNES. The remains of Mr. John Anderson, landlord of the Railway and Commercial lintel, Widnes, who died on Thursday week, were interred at Farnworth Parisn Church, on Sunday afternoon, in the presence of a large number of spectators. The funeral cortege consisted of 15 coachesand a hearse,and amongst those %rho followed the deceased to the grave was a deputation from the Foot- ball Club, and a deputation of workmen from Messrs. Pilkingtons', where the deceased had been employed. Nearly the whole of the publicans of the town were pre- sent, besides a number of other friends. 'flic surial service was conducted by the Rev. J. Leigh, cat.

WIDNES FREE 'ABEAM: Com:Aim:E. The ordinary meeting of this Committee was held in the Town Hall, Widnes, on Wednesday, presided over by Mr. H. Wade Deacon. Miss Proctor, tlic librarian, sub- mitted her monthly report. She said the total atte:ulance for the month was 11,944, which gave a daily average of 497. The penny rate realized £443. Accounts amounting to £lO4 6s. 4d. were passed for parnant, including £27 16s for annual repayment of principal and interest, 4;15 12s. for cleaning, and £l2 19s, 7d, for Nolo.

A DA:WM-tors Frusn4gin Ar WIONTP. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, William Evans, of 10 Beaumont-street, was charged with assaulting his wife Ann. The defendant pleaded guilty, and it was intimated that application for a judicial separation would be made. Mr. Knowles, who appeared for the complain- ant, said his client was a young woman, 22 years of age, and was only married to the defendant in October,of last year. After they had been married a fortnight the de- fendant ran at his wife and assaulted her, and three weeks later he insisted on sleeping with a razor under his pillow. He also calmly and deliberately, not in a pas- sion, threatened to kill her. Up to Saturday, the Bth inst., this state of things continued, and when ke came home on that day after having his tea he took his knife out of his pocket and said he would cut her throat. He then tried to persuade her to go to bed, as he wanted to cut her throat. On the following Monday he threw her out of the house, struck Iler, and again threatened to kill her. He had offered to give her 12s. a week. He (Mr. Knowles) did not ask for that sum, but would be satsified with from 7s. 6d. to 10s. per week. The woman said she was continually in terror of her life, and the Bench had power under the Act to grant a separation order, which he applied for. The complainant was then sworn, and corroborated the statement of her solicitor. He was generally in drink, and only allowed her four or five shillings a week.—The defendant : I have nothing to say. I admit that all she says is true.—Mr. Knowles : I understand he has been a soldier 2—The defendant : I have served in India.—Mr. Knowles : It may be the hot climate has affected him, and the drink as well. The magistrates retired for a few minutes to consider their decision, and on re-entering the court the Chairman I said: You will have to go to goal for one month, and a separation order will be granted. When you come out of gaol you will have to contribute 7s. 6d. a week towards your wife's maintenance. We consider your wife's safety is in peril. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at an hours' notiee.- . W. _ EDDISBURY DIVISION OF CHESHIRE. On Saturday afternoon a meeting of Conservativ,isl and Liberal Unionists ef the Eddisbury Division of Cheshire was held at the Chester Conservative Club, for the purpose of considering the communication. from Mr. H. J. Tollemache, M.P., relative to his retiring from the representation of Eddisbury at the end of the present Parliament. A very strong feel- ing prevailed amongst those present that every effort should be made to induce Mr. Pollemache to reconsider his determination. As a result of the expression ot such feeling, Mr. Tollemache con- sented to do so, and placed his services at the disposal of his party should an early election occur. THE GLAZEIMOOE RANGE. Colonel Blundell, M.P., on Tuesday received from the War Office, the reply of the Government to the applica.non of the Manchester voters in the matter of the Glazebrook Range, tite letter was at once forwarded to the Brigadier-Major Lieu-Colonel Luby. Its purport as was anticipated in this column last week, is a definite refusal of the request fora loan, on the ground that the security proposed does not satisfy the requirements of the law. A meeting of commanding officers will doubtless be held to consider the letter at an early date, but Colonel Blundell is satisfied that any further pres- sure upon the 'Government would be useless. UsatnELLss na-covaaxn at an bonnet notice.—J. lc W. Dutton, San key-street. RAILWAY RATES INQUIRY. Among the witnesses examined,on Wednesday, at the Railway Rates Inquiry at Westminster were Mr. Pickering, of Messrs. Blundell's Pemberton collieries, and Mr. Alfred Hewlett, managing director of the Wigan Coal and Iron Company- The latter said his Company paid at present for railway carriage £150,000 a year, and the proposed increase in the terminal charges would increase that amount by 15 per cent. On the average, the effect of all the changes proposed by the railway companies on traffic for distances under twenty-three miles would be to rather more than double the existing rates. Mr. Jeans, secretary of the Iron and Steel Institute, hav- ing addressed the Court on behalf of the industries he represented, the inquiry was again adjourned. THE CHEMICAL TRADE AT WIDNES. Owing to the strike of dock labourers at Liver- pool, the Flatmen's Association has issued a notice that all flatmen shall refuse to load coal, chemicals, or any kind of cargo whatever, for non-Union ships. The Association consists of 1,000 members, and the whole trade of Widnes is affected. A large number of flatmen have in consequence of the notice, re- fused to take cargoes to vessels worked by imported men. The manufacturers of the town are, however, threatened with a more serious difficulty through the dispute between the colliers and their em- ployers. Should a strike take place, neatly the whole of the works in the town will be stopped. The Chemical Workers' Union, organised by Mr. I P. J. Kidg, now numbers about 000 members. THE COAL MINES REGULATION ACT. At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, Arthur Wright, a collier, living at 348, Parr-st., St. Helens, was summoned for a breach a the Coal Mines Regulation Act by havingin his possession matches, a pipe, and tobacco in the flavannah Colliery, Parr, belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. Mr. 3.0. Swift (St. Helens) prosecuted, and stated that the defendant was a drawer, and on the 14th ult the underlooker, a man named Jacob Potter, found a pipe and tobacco and some matches in lie coat pocket. He spoke to the defendant about it, and The latter said it was pure forgetfulness on his part. Ile had apparently forgot to take them out of his pocket before going ,down the mine, and the pro- prietors had no reason to doubt the defendant's word in i,hat respect. A fine of Sc. and costs was imposed. • CRITCHLEY, High Class Tailor. Bold-st.Warrington.—.Adrt.

TRIPLETS. Mrs. Edwards, wife of Evan Edwards, a glass worker, residing at Ravenhead. St. Helens, gave birth to three daughters on Friday morning. The mother and children are all in a healthy 'condition. The parents are both members of the Salvation Army. The Rev. H. S. Bolton, vicar of Ravenhead, has, is stated, made application for the Queen's Bounty. KAY.B TIC PILLS, specific in Neuralgia. Face-ache, 91d., and 131 d. ; postage 10.0 Of all Chemists.—Adet.

. - MR. W. CM/WIELD FOR LINCOLN. Referring to Mr. W. Crostield as a candidate for Lincoln, the "Liverpool Daily Post" says :--" It was remarked when the poll at Sleaford was announced that such a return boded well for Mr. William Crosfield's prospects at Lincoln. Such antici- pations will be more than confirmed by the result at Stamford, and indeed it may no be confidently hoped that the advent of such a thoroughly good Liverpool Liberal to the House of Commons is assured as soon as an opportunity offers." GO TO TICK WLNA.I.LIE CfCLE CO. tor racing machines and light roadsters.—Advt.

TRH 11011 E IRON TRADE. The English iron market is quieter, if anything, and its tendency is still downwards. Very little is being done in pig-iron, makers holding on pretty firmly to their quotations while users generally purchase-of merchants. Scotch warrants are again lower on the week, the result being that makers in Scotland have reduced their prices from 6d. to 28. a ton, according to brand. Middlesbrough pig-iron has lost Is. 3d.. a ton, In other districts prices of pig-iron are easier. Although makers of hematite pig are putting into practice their agreement of blowing out furnaces, to counteract the effects of operations in warrants, they have had to lower their quotation 3s. a ton. Manufactured iron is unsettled, and very little business is put through. The market is easier on the whole, merchants offering under makers' prices, and in the north of England ship plates and angles have fallea,—/ron
A FOOTBALL DRESSING Room ON FIRS.
.. --- • A singular fire occurred at the Running Horses Hotel, Liverpool-road, St. Helens, on Saturday after- noon. The hotel is the he.adquarters of the St. _ • .

. . Helens Association Football Clib, and on the occa- sion ot football Matches one of the rooms is used as a dressing-room for the teams. , This was done on Saturday afternoon last, when the visiting team was the Golborne F.C. Just before the players left the room to go upon the field, some of the men be- gait larking, and a pipe which one of them was smoking fell upon ~some of the clothes which the players had taken off. The pipe was picked up, the players and friends left the room, and the door was locked, everything being, apparently, safe. When the playersveturned from the field,, however, it was found that the room was on fire. A dense volume of smoke issued from it, and it was after- wards found that several articles of clothing had been damaged, is form was burned, and trousers be- longing to a Golborne player were entirely des- troyed. This occasioned a deal of humorous sym- pathy, and a collection among the friends present resulted in the purchase of a new pair of trousers for the unfortunate owner of those destroyed. CRITCULEY, Practical Tailor, Bold-st.,Warrington.—Adrf.

div.head: RUNCORN RU R S 41N ITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RU R S 41N ITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Colonel 'Ashton presided and there were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, and Messrs. J. Knowles, J. Stokes. J. Whitlow, T. Lewis, J. Baguley, J. Bran- dreth, P. llall, E. Aaron, C. Motinfield ; IL Linaker (clerk), H. G. Linaker (assistant clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer), and Farrington (nuisance inspec-, Bran OFFICER'S REVOIVT.—Itt Ids report Dr. Adams stated that there were two cases of diptheria one at Frodsham Lor ;ship, and another at Helsby Hill, Helsby, while in Frodsham a child two years old had been attacked, and had died from the disease. In the latter ease the mother had been nursing a child in Liverpool which was suffering from diptheria and had in this manner orought infection with her. Several fresh cases of scarlet fever had occurred at Frod- sham on premises on which he had previously notified that disease had occurred. He had also to report two cases of typhoid fever which had occurred at Frodsham. —ln answer to Mr. Brandreth, Dr. Adams said his duties had been very much increased by the new act. Since the 9th December last when the Act had been first put into force he had received close upon 40 notificalons, al- though during the whole of last year he only reneived 26 notifications from all sources. RE-APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER.—The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner moved that Dr. Adams be reappointed medical officer at a salary of £l2O for the ensuing year. —The Assistant Clerk said he had received a letter from Mr. Brandreth intimating that he intended to move that Dr. A. J. Briant, of Helsby, be appointed medical officer. —The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner said Dr. Adams had given entire satisfaction, and he was sorry to hear that opposi- tion was to be raised to his t ppointrnent.—Mr. Stokes seconded the proposal of the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner.—The Chairman asked Mr. Brandreth if he had given notice $ all tbe Guardians of his intention to move the amend- ment—Mr. Brandreth said he had not.—The Chairman questioned whether in that case he could put it to the Board.—Mr. Brandreth suggested that the appointment might be left over till notice had been given to all the Guardians. He had known nothing of Mr. Tanner's motion or he should have given notice at the same time. His reason for moving the appointment of Dr. Briant was that he was a Young man, and he lived in a part of the Union, and paid rates and taxes to the Union. Dr. 13riant attended to the poor of the Union from many of whom he got no pay, and he (Mr. Brandreth) considered he was the best person to appoint, and ought to have preference over one who lived out of the Union. He wished it to be understood, however, that he had nothing to say against the manner in which Dr. Adams had dis- charged his duties.—The Chairman thought it would be a bad precedent to discharge at a moment's notice an officer who had done his duty.-.—The Rev. J. W. N. Termer said the Local Government Board objected to the appointment of a medical officer residing in the Union and having private practice.—Mr. Knowles thought it was better to have an independent man.—The Chairman then ruled that the amendment could not be put, and only three voted for amotion that the business of appoint- ing a medical officer be adjourned. Dr. Adams was then , re-appointed. • CLaines Seramy.—The Clerk's salary for the past year was fixed at £B5. OVERCROWDING.—Mr. Farrington reported a case of overcrowding at Appleton Cross in asanall house contain- ing two rooms. The total number of inmates in the house at each weekend was 18. It was resolved that notice be served for the abatement of the nuisance.

div.head: PRESENTATIONS TO ODDFELLOWS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: PRESENTATIONS TO ODDFELLOWS AT RUNCORN.

The members and friends of the Rose of Sharon Lodge, G.U.0.0. to the number of 200 sat down to an ample tea prepared by the committee Brothers Douglas, Hiszlehurst, Jones, Lambert, Iliadley, Rutter, Rogerson, and Whinyates, in the Bethesda Schoolroom on Saturday: The tea tables were pre- sided over by the Misses Hindley, Horabin and Stringer, and Mesdames Dyer, Ilazlehurst. Leath- wood, Jones, Hindley, Massey, Rogerson and Rutter. After spending an enjoyable hour in discussing the good things provided by the committee, which gave every satisfaction,the tables were cleared and the chair was taken by Bro. John Rogerson., who in his address said, after having referred to the presence of ladies, that in his opinion their fraternity owed a deep debt of grati- tude to the members wives, and a great many men who were Oddfellows would not he so had it not been for the prudence and forethought of the industrious partners who had joined them in the battle of life. (Applause.) They had met to recognise the services of two well tried officials. (Applause.) He would have them understand that those two were not the only officials whom they re- cognised as having brought the lodge to its present sound position., but they were the two oldest. (Applause.) The Misses Pope and Ilorsfall then gave a pianoforte duet which was received with great favour and they kindly repeated in reply to calls for an encore. Mies Fogg sang with good judgment and effect " Loves Golden Dream,' and her charming rendering created repeated calls for a further song, and she kindly gave " Truest love." Mr. F. Scott's inimitable rendering of " Sister Mary walks like that" pleased theaudiencegreatly, and hr war of encorehe sang " Dearly .beloved bretl i re& " in his usuai comic vein. Mr. John Leattierwood was in good voice and gave "The Waritir Bold with true pathisA and in reply to calls for an encore he itacg " Then voiell, remember me," with good effect.—Bro. 'limo. Davies' characteristic singing of "Measure your wants by your means," and his encore "The Bey can say Pane," fairly brought. down the house. Time Ckaorman then called on Brother William Cliff, Pre- tom who said they all knew the efforts Bro. Thomas Booth had made on behalf of the Lodge, how hard he had worked and how he had never lost an opportunity of gaining; recruits to the lodge and he was quite certain no one had brought more young .men into the lodge. (Applause.) For 25 years he had served id the offices of the lodge, seven years as treasurer, 12 years as trustee, and six years in the minor offices, and had given great satisfaction by his invariable kindness and attention, and it wee his pleasing duty to ask Bro. Booth to come on the platform and receive a handsome marble timepiece on which they saw a suitableinscription on a silver plate, and together with that they presented him with an 'emblem of the order as slight tokens of their apprecia- tion. (Loud applause.) Bro. Thomas Booth said it was with feelings of great gratitude, that he received their kind tokens of recognition of his twenty-five years ser- vice. It had always been his endeavour since he joined the lodge 32 years ago to do his utmost and his work ' spoke for itself.. (Applause.) Mr. Frank Scott then , gave" In the Asylum,'? hi fine style, and sang as encore the song " Mother-ht-lays" with great zest. Mr. R. . Musgrove's rendering of a " pianoforte solo displayed a

large acquaintaned"WithllM capabilities of the instru- ment and a good knowledge of music, his efforts being received with loud applause. Upon the call of the Chairman. Bro. Edward Jones said he had a pleas- ing duty to perform. That was to ask the Chairman on behalf of the members to present a handsome marble timepiece and an emblem of the order to Bro. Thomas [Davies as slight tokens of their appreciation of 33 years h service in the lodge, 20 years as secretary and 13 years in various offices. (Applause.) A short time ago Parlia- ment ordered an enquiry into the working of Friendly Societies and as a result of that it was found that those carried on by workingmen were carried on in a business like way, and as a result societies like theirs had not been interfered with while others had had to accept various restrictions. That showed that the societies had good officers and that night they were met to recognise the services of two of them. (Applause.) Bro. T. Davies, who was received with loud applause, acknowledged the gifts in suitable language, and said he lsoked on those presentations as recognition of 20 years' doietnright hard work, and he was glad to say that he was still in harness and intended to keep in a little longer. (Applause.) They had a Ist of young men in the lodge who were well educated,:and who had had a better start than the older members, and they were taking advantage of that start. (Hear, hear.) They had had to work their society up and had not had 20 years hard work without making a mistake; however, they were now on the right line. (Applause.) The lodge funds, January Ist, 1870, were £607 18s., and December 31st, 1889, £2,455 9s. 2d. The District Funeral Fund, December 31st, 1889, was £Bl6 17s. 4d. During the past 20 years they had initiated 493 new members, -had paid £2,400 for sick pay, £530 for members' deaths, £370 for members' wives £24 widows, and £283 17s. for mem- bers' children. 4pplause.)—Bro. Rutter proposed a vote of thanks to the ladies and gentlemen who had provided the entertainment, and Bro. Erndley proposed a vote of thanks to the ladies and gentlemen who had worked se hard and provided them such a substantial tea. Both resolutions were passed with applause, and a most enjoy- able evening was concluded with the singing of the National Anthem.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. Mowney.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Majer flazleburst. PITCH AND Toss.—John McCann, Thomas Woodfine, and Thomas Flannigan, youths, were charged with playing pitch and toss on the 2nd inst., on the evidence of P.C. Woodrow.—The defendants were each fined is., and costs Bs. 6d. FOOTBALL IN THE STREET.—AIbert Abel, Arthur annul, John Ingham, and H. Peacoek, youths, were summoned for playing football in Fox-st. Mr. Barton, who appeared for Abel, explained the circumstances, and the defendants were ordered to pay the costs, Bs. 6d. each. CHIMNIES ON FlRE.—William birch, Church-st., and John Dutton, of Greenway-road, were each tined 6d. and costs for permitting the chimnies of their dwellings -fob° on fire. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. Jane Drury and John O'Neil were each fined 10s. and costs for being drunk and disorderly ; and for a similar offence Henry Penketh Mather was fined 10s. and costs.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THOESDAY.—Before Mr. W. L. M`Clure and Major Gaskell. MISCELLANEOLGL—Ann Walsh, North-st. (25th appear- ance), was fined ss. and costs for being drunk, and for a similar offence Jos. Killalea, High-st., was fined 7s. 6d. and costs and John Taylor, Widnes-road, ss. and costs. A number of persons were summoned for not sending their children regularly to school and the usual fine of Sc. was imposed in each case.--Patrick Ryan, of SankeV- st., was bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, for fighting in Messrs. Hutchinson's works.— Wm. McAuley, was fined is. aud costs and Robert McAuley and Peter Lightfoot were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs for playing pitch and toss in Ash-row. DOG CASES.—William Killain, of Marshall-road, Joseph Bradshaw, Hurst-st. ; and Thomas Burroughs, 12, West-st., were each fined 7s. 6d. and costs for keeping a dog without a license. Peter Blackburn, Ball-lane, and Patrick Gill, Chester-road. were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs for allowing their dogs to be at large unmuzzled.— Sydney B. Bennett, of Widnes-road, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for allowing his dog to be at large, insecurely I muzzled. The animal while wearing a muzzle bit a boy named Edward pixies on the A BAD TANANT.—On the application of Mr. Knowles, solicitor, the Bench granted an ejectment order against George Worth, the tenant of a house belonging to Mr. William Longton, at Ditton. The rent was 3s. Sid. per week, and the arrears amounted to £5 17s. 6d., and Worth would neither Leave the house nor pay the rent. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—Margaret Power and Mary McNulty. of Pear-st., were summoned for assaulting Mary Sutton on the Ist inst.—The case was dismissed.

RUNCORN' POLICE COURT. WEDNEDAY.—Before Mr. James Handley and Mr. James Reynolds. 1 Mitratt.—Edward Howe and John Flannigan, were , each fined 10s. and costs for being drunk while in charge of a horse. Richard Thomas, a sailor, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk. WANDERING ABROAD.—James Capper and George Ed. Capper, boys, were charged with wannering abroad without visible means of subsistence. The boys were found that morning sleeping on the premises of the Salt Union, at Weston Point, and said they had been sent out by their father, who lived in Fryer-st. The father denied and alleged that he had been out of work for weeks past. and a person had promised to find the boys a lodg- ing free of charge.—The boys were discharged on condi- tion that they went to the Workhouse. BAD LANGDAGR.—For using bad langutge in Pool-lane, Helen Barker was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, 15s. 4d., or seven days in default.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held I at the Workhouse,Dutton,on Tuesday. Colonel Ash- I ton presided, and there were present the Rev. J. W. Tanner. Messrs. Grice, Taylor, Aaron, Stokes, Lewis, Hall, W. Whitlow, Brandreth, Knowles, Baguley, Jones, Mounfield, Jeff, H. Linaker (clerk), and 11. G. Linaker (assistant clerk). THE Comma EtecrioNs.---The fee of the returning officer for conducting the forthcoming elections was fixed at £2O. UNVACCINATED CRILDREN.—The Workhouse Master reported that the Medical Inspector of the Local Govern- ment Board had visited the Workhouse, and had called attention to the fact that two boys and one girl were unvaccinated. The attention of the Medical Officer had been called to the fact. Is WORK SO ABUNDANT ?—Some conversation took place as to the number of able-bodied paupers in the Workhouse, as one or two of the members stated that work could be very easily obtained outside the Work- house just now. Mr. Whitlow said that no man need be in want just now. Farmers were wanting workmen,yet hundreds of tramps passed along the road and never asked for it. In answer to a question the Workhouse Master said if he refused anybody admission to the Workhouse he would have to do it on his own respoesi- idlity. Nearly all the orders for admission that were brought to the Workhouse were issued by the relieving efficers at Frodsham and Runcorn, or by Mr. Earp, who was an overseer. Mr. Stokes thought that people had no right to go and trouble Mr. Earp for these orders. Not knowing what desperate characters he had to deal with, Mr. Earp would net like to refuse the orders. The Clerk said it was one of the Overseer's duties to give these orders. Mr. Whitlow thought that the Workhouse was made a sort of lodging-house of by many people, some of whom were passing from one part of the Ship Canal to another. The Clerk said that a great many who represented themselves as Ship Canal men wonla not work anywhere. The Workhouse Master having described the task that was sett, tramps, Mr. Taylor said he knew that that Workhouse had not a good name amongst people of that class. He had heard of a con- versation between three et feur of them, in which one advised the others to give the place a wide berth. The discussion then dropped. -

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Winston, on Thursday afternoon, when there were present Mr. J. W. Wareing (deputy chairman) who presided, the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Messrs. G. E. Chadwick, J. Buckley. .T. Mercer, J. Barchall, J. Kenwright, P. Longton, J. Whal- ley, G. Davies. R. A. Graves, J. Ranson, J. Marsh, W. Middlehurst, W. Lowe, W. Burrows, W. Daine, J. Leatherharrow, C. B. Johnson, W. Tyrer, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). RF.LIEF. —Mr. Hale, the Workhouse Master, reported that there were 588 inmates this week, 604 last week. 590 in the corresponding week last year ; 55 vagrants had been relieved, and 77 in the corresponding week last

year. THE Retirsvina OFFICER'S DISECTE.—The minutes of the Visiting Committee stated at a meeting on the 3rd inst., they had under consideration the dispute which had arisen between Mr. William Bullock, relieving officer for the Prescot district, and his brother, Mr. James Bullock, in respect to the payment of the latter who had, for some weeks, officiated as assistant relieving officer. The brothers were called betore the Cemmittee, but an intimation was conveyed to the Committee that the matter in dispute had been amicably settled, and it was unanimously decided that the case was not one for the intervention of the Guardians.—The minutes were passed. THE OFFICERS' RAIIONS.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board in reply to one from the Guard- ians asking consent to the payment of 24. 61. per week to each officer of the Workhouse in addition to the pre- sent ration allowance. The Board assented to the pro- posal for 12 months but requested that in the meaaime the matter might be further considered. The letter was referred to the Visiting Committee. RAINHILL ASYLUIf.--A letter was read from Mr. Wm. Swift, solicitor, Liverpool, clerk to the Rainhill County Asyluin Visiting Justices intimating that he was instructed to inform the Guardians that it would be inconvenient for them to retain the private clothing of patients sent to the institution and further that they had not accommodation for storing the same. The letter continued : " With regard to recent escapes from the

Asylum the Committtee have further instructed me ter inform the Guardians, that they are taking steps to prevent, as far as possible, such escapes in the future." —The Chairman remarked that he thought the Asylum Authorites ought to provide accommodation for the storage of patients clothing.—Mr. Middlehurst said the present system interfered very much with the work of the relieving officers, who had to take the clothing of patients to and from the Asylum and Workhouse. He thought the Guardians ought to press the matter for- ward.—Mr. llurchall thought that if the grievance was brought before the Asylum authorities in a proper manner it would be remedied.—The Clerk said the present system prevailed all over the country but looking at it from a ratepayer's point of view he thought the Asyl urn authori- ties ought to take charge of their patients clothes.—Ha pointed out that that the letter did not contain a direct refusal to do so, and after some discussion it was finally decided that the Clerk should again communicate with them upon the subject.

- - . THREATENED STRIKE ON COLLIERS.—The Clerk read the following letter, dated the 6th March. "Dear Sir,— vire beg to give you this early intimation that the whole of our men have given notice that they will cease work on the 15th inst. If this is carried out the whole of our supplies will be entirely cut off from that date.—Yours 'truly, RICHARD EVANS AND Co., Limited."—The Clerk stated that one of the conditions of the contract enabled the Guardians to purchase against the firm if it was necessary.—The Chairman: lam afraid you will find it very difficult to buy against them. The trouble is where to buy.—Mr. Buckley: The warm weather is coming, and we shall not very much trouble them —The Clerk: I think we shall be able to get the coal.—The matter then dropped. KIRICDALE SCHOOLS.—The Re\r. S. A. K. Sylvester, re- ported that a Committee of Guardians visited the schools at Kirkdale last week. They went very carefully through all the buildings, playgrounds, Ix., and had the whole of the children brought before them. They were very pleased with the state in which they found them, and they found everything carried out just as. the Board would wish. (hear, hear.)

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

_ The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P. presided, and there were present Messrs. T. Handley, J. Midwood, J. Cook, F. Liddell, F. Reyes, D. Wright B. Brown, H. Timmis, J. Taylor, J. Houghton, S. Sadler, Dr. O'Beeffe. with J. T. Allen (clerk), L Carr (engineer), J. Dickson (sanitary inspector.)

div.head: SHIP C&NAL AND BRINE SCHEME,
div.p: THE SHIP C&NAL AND BRINE SCHEME,

The Chafr—r;a-n—L- said Mr. Oppenheim of St. Helens, was present, to consult with the members about the Man- chester Ship Canal and the Widnes Brine Company, and he informed him that it was a private matter. It was not deemed expedient that it should be made public at present, and he hoped the press would not feel he was doing anything improper by asking them to retire for a short time. The matter would afterwards be made perfectly public.—On the proposition of Mr. Handley seconded by Mr. Midwood, the meeting was resolved in- to Committee.

THE APPOINTMENT OF. SURVEYOR. The Chairman said the first business was the appoint- ment of a surveyor. A Committee appointed by the Board had selected the following seven out of a 167 ap- plicants, te have a personal interview :—John Paterson, age 35, Sheffield ; Thos. W. Franks, age 30, West Brom- wich ; Fdk. W. Walker, age 35, Warrington; W. L. Bothwell, age 36, Hindley ; John S. Sinclair, age 34, Bootle; D. Waterhouse, age 32, Worksop ; Hugh Nettle- ton, age 38, Leeds. • -

ALLEGED ILLEGALITY. Dr. O'Keeffe said an old member of the Board had told him that there was a resolution on the books that appointments of this kind should be made by the Board. —Mr. Wright road a resolution to that effect passed in 1882,—The Clerk said the Board were perfectly in order in chputing a committee to act in the matter.—Dr. O'Keeffe contended that they had no right to do so with- out suspending the standing orders, and that was not done. The proceedings up to the present were both irregular and illegal.—Mr. Handley- said the course taken was a proper one and in accordance with the resolution. —Dr. O'Keeffe The Board has stultified itself.—The Chairman: I don't think the Board has done anything of the sort.—Dr. O'Keeffe moved that the Board take legal opinion on the matter before proceeding further.— Mr. Wright seconded the proposition, because he did not think the Board had acted legally.—Only the mover and seconder voted for the motion, and the action of the ' Board was confirmed.

SIR. TAYLOR MALES AN EXPLANATION. Mr. Taylor remarked that anything said about him affected him as little as pouring water on a duck's back, but there was a statement made at a public meeting a week ago that he must flatly contradict. The statement was that he had received £lO of the ratepayers' money for work in connection with a certain sewer. He had rot received a single farthing one way or another. As to other statements, he knew nothing about them ; it was mere electioneering. THE SUCCESSFUL CANDIDATE. After intervi2wing the candidates Mr. Taylor moved, and Mr. Liddell seconded, the appointment of Mr. Sin- clair. and Mr. Sadler moved, and Mr. Houghton se- conded, the appointment of Mr. Waterhouse.—On a vote being taken, Mr. Sinclair was elected by seven votes to five. The successful candidate was then called into the room, and was congratulated by the Chairman upon his appointment. THREATENED STRIKE OF COLLIERS. Mr. D. Wright moved the adoption of the minutes of the Gas and Water Committee, and remarked that there was the probability of a strike amongst the colliers in the district, and in order to make provision against it Mr. Carr had arranged that by the 15th inst, the Board should have in stock aboutl,l23 tons of coal and cannell which was equal to five weeks supply of gas. There would also be provided 17 days supply of coal at Netherley Pumping Station, and seven days supply at Stockswell. Before this time expired the Committee hoped that sonA amicable arrangement would be come to between the colliers and their masters.—Mr. Taylor- seconded the motion.—Carried.

HIGHWAY MATTERS. The minutes of the Highway Committee contained various items with regard to public improvements. The following buNding plans had been examined and- approved :—Twci houses, Albert-rd., for J. Dagnall ; ten houses, Ross-st., for Runcorn nopertv Co.; Baptist Chapel, Deacon-rd., subject to ventilating pipes being shown. It was recommended that the following streets at Moss Bank be made, sewered, &c. under section 150 of the P.R. Act, 1875, also the back passages and ap- - preach passages in connection with the said streets, viz., Elizabeth-st.. Mary-st., and Brown-st.--Mr. Sadler moved and Mr. Houghton seconded the adoption of the minutes.

TEE TIPPING OF COAL. Mr. Taylor drew attention to a letter which had been, sent out by the Committee to coal dealers informing them that if diligence be observed in removing coals tipped on the roadway and footpath no action would be taken.— Mr. Wright contended that under these circumstances the resolution of the Bond that no coal should be tipped on the footpaths of the town, should be rescinded.—Mr. Sadler said it was optional whether the Board took action or otherwise. Perhaps t''e original resolution was too strong and overstepped the mark. It was not necessary to rescind the resolution, but simply to state that no action would be taken if the coal were removed in a reasonable time.—Carried.

HEALTH COMMITTEE. The Medical Officer reported to this Committee thatE during February. there were 88 births and 60 deaths, being at the respective rates of 32.2 and 24. per 1,000, 14 deaths occurred amongst children under one yeax and seven between one and five years. There were six inquests. No death from zymotic disease occurred during the month. The high death rate is due to the number of persons over 25 years of age who have died from bronchitis and pneumonia, probably consequent on the prevalence of influenza. Twenty-five notifications of infectious disease have been received during February, including fourteen casesof scarlatina and five of typhoid or enteric fever. There were 5 patients in the Accident Hospital and 8 in the Fever Hospital. DONATIONS TO HOSPITALS.

Mr Wright moved the adoption of the minutes and said during the past year very many valuable and use- ful articles had been given to both hospitals, and he proposed that the thanks of the Board be conveyed to the donors.—Mr. Carey seconded.—Carried.
THE FIRE ENGINE STATION.

A letter was read from Mr. Shelmerdine referring to the plans of the fire engii el house and 14 cottages pro- posed to be built by the Board, with the consent of the trustees of the Leigh estate. The solicitors thought the proposed buildings unobjectionable, but concluded that the Local Board would require a formal consent.—The Clerk dndertook to deal with the matter.

div.head: NEW MANUFACTORY FOR. FARNWORTH.
div.p: NEW MANUFACTORY FOR. FARNWORTH.

Mr. W. Curran Barrett, estate agent of Manchester, wrote stating that a client of his contemplated the erec- tion or renting of works at Farnworth, near Widnes. for the manufacture of sulphonic acid. He would feeL obliged if he could inform him whether the Local Board would or could object to this builness being carried on. —The Clerk sail he haa referred the writer to his solicitor. (La ughter.) TEE MOSS BANK SEVER DISPUTE,

The Clerk read a letter from Messrs. S. Cowburn contractor, re the Boards offer in connection with their Moss Bank sewn- account. They could not for - a moment understand why such an offer should have been made to them. They were quite in the, dark, as to how the deduction was arrived at, and as the Board did not say whatthe deduc- tion was for, they thought they were justly entitled to a, statement showing how the deduction is arrived at as they could not see any reason why they should suffer any loss at all on the account, and it was most 'unfair that they should be kept out of their money so long. They hoped to he favoured with an early remittance of the account.—Mr. Sadler said a resolution had been passed by the Board that an engineer should be called in, with power to open out the sewer and report upon it.— The Chairman : And that recommendation stands when it is 2—Mr. Sadler: Yes.
_ FINANCE. On the proposition of Mr. I% Handley, accounts amounting to ' £14,201 Cs. recommeded by the Finance Committee were passed for payment.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES
NEGLECT OF FAMILY.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, a man named James Charnock was charged with having left his three children chargeable to the Union. It was stated that during the last 12 months he and his family had cost the ratepayers about £4O. He was sent to pri- son for two months._ ___

div.head: CHASING A WIVII.
div.p: CHASING A WIVII.

A horsekeeper' named William Patton, who lives in Queen-St., was before the Warrington magistrates, on Monday, on a charge of wife assault. The evidence against him was to the effect that on Sunday night he chased his wife about the town with the avowed inten- tion of assaulting her. She appealed to the police for protection, and a constable accompunied her home. Whilst he was there prisoner knocked his wife on to& chair, and threatened to assault the policeman with a poker. The Bench sent prisoner to gaol for two months, with hard labour.

div.head: VIOLENT DRt'NKARD.
div.p: A VIOLENT DRt'NKARD.

On Tuesday, at the Warrington Police Court, a middle- aged man named James McCann was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Mersey-st. on the previous afternoon, and alga with assaulting William Hall at the same time and place. From the evidence it appeared that the prisoner had been drinking at a public- house in Mersey-at., and began to quarrel about the change he received id 'payment for some drink. On being remonstrated with the prisoner struck Hall a violent blow on the mouth, and when taken into custody assaulted two policemen on the way to the Police Station. A fine of 20s. and costs was inflicted, or in default 14 days hard labour.
A aENTLEMAN WHO CARRIED • Borns ASKED THE Bus-
DILIVER TO HATS A DION".

Joseph Curran, a 'bus-driver, appeared at the War- rington Police Court, on Monday, to answer a summons charging him with having been drunk whilst in charge of two herses and a 'bus, on the 3rd inst. The evidence was to the effect that the defendant, who was in charge of a 'bus running between Warrington and Stockton Heath, was so mnch under the influence of drink that had it not been for a strap that fastened him to his seat he would have fallen off. Defendant told the magis- trates that a gentleman who got on the 'bus at Stockton Heath had a bottle, and gave him a drink from it. The •drink must either have been very strong, or drugged. A fine of 55., including costs, was imposed.
CONFIRMED TOPER FAILS TO wNYINCE THE HENCE{ OF HIS GOOD INTENTIONS. •

Danielerosby, whose " character "sheet records over , three score appearances at the Warrington Police Court, is a man who speaks fair and promises much, but fails most miserably in the carrying outof his goodintentions. When in trouble, of course, his chief aim is to get out of it as soon as he can, but he is Very unsuccessful in his efforts to keep out. He was again in the dock on Mon- day, on the usual charge of "drunk and disorderly," to which he answered a -kind of half-and-half plea. He admitted having had some drink, but repudiated the police evidence that he was very drunk. A friend, he said, wanted to take him into a public house and give him a pint, but he would not accept it, and, therefore, as a matter of course, he could not have been drunk. The Magistrates' Clerk mentioned that priseners' brother was at one time a very regular offender, and at last he was sent to a lunatic asylum. Prisoner promised that be would take the pledge, and keep it, but the Bench reminded him that he had already signed it twice. This time, prisoner replied, he would " filful" his promise, but the magistrates were sceptical and sent him to prison for a month, the Mayor remarking that they could not have the Court turned into a laughing stock by the prisoner coming there every fortnight. If he did not care for his freedom, he must not expect the Bench to do so.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

DnrsranwEss.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon a man named Crilly for having been drunk in Wilderspool-road on the previous night. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), and Aldermen Davies, Harrison, and Sutton. Ibitnwitx:iskss.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—George Hopkins, in Hardy-st.. on Saturday evening, dismissed with a caution; Daniel Crosby, in Buttermarket-st. on Saturday night, sent to prison for a month ; Julia Ball, at Market-gate, on Satur- day night, ordered to pay the costs 4s. ; John Jones, in Haydock-st., on Sunday night. fined ss. including costs; John Cochrane, in Percival's-fold, fined 55., including .costs; William Marsh, in Bewsey-road, on the 2nd inst., fined ss. including costs ' • James Finn, in Naylor-A.. on the Ist inst., dismissed with a reprimand; Mary Brennan, in Silver-square, on the 3rd inst., dismissed; Thomas Champion, in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday sight, fined ss. including costs, and ordered to pay 3s. 6d. for damage done in the shop uf William Lythgoe, confectioner. THE Paseoxstnitmrs OF DOG OW:Mtg.—Richard Higham was fined ss. and costs for keeping a dog with- out having taken out a license, and William Dutton, for allowing a dog belonging tohim to beat largeunmuzzled, was fined 55., including costs. ?rufous DRIVINTh—John Baguley, summoned for ltaving furiously driven a horse and cart, in Sankey-st., ort the first inst., was fined 25. 64., including costs. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—James Leslie, for allowing the chimney of his house to be on fire, was, ordered to pay one shilling. DRUNK Wrmsr IN CHARGB.—James Rush, for having been drunk whilst in charge of two horses and a lurry, in Rnutsford-rd., on the 3rd inst., was fined 55., includ-

ing costs. SASITARY PROSECIITIONS.—Ed ward Woodcock,and John H. Fleming, jun., were summoned for having allowed certain liquid filth to run out of a cart in Mersey-st., on the sth March. Woodcock was in charge of the cart, and Mr. Fleming was summoned as the owner. The Bench dismissed the case against the carter, and fined the owner 10s. and costs. STREET ORSTRUCTIONS._SamueI Lawless, fishmonger, Buttermarket-St, was ordered to pay the costs for having allowed a load of coal to be tipped in front of his resi- dence after nine a.m., contrary to the live-laws. A similar summons against the Rev. Father Sumner was dealt with in the same way.—Edward Norman, Friar's- green, was fined 2.5. 6d. including costs for having allowed a handcart to remain in Bold-st. for 35 minutes.— For having left a bag of soot and a sweeping machine on the footpath in Bold-st., for 45 minutes, Peers Marsh was fined 55. including costs. TIIESDAT.—Befoye Messrs. W. Owen and E. M. Crosfield. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence Martha McCann was sent to goal for seven days, and John Connor was fined ss. and costs or seven days' imprisonment. ScHoot CASE3.—The folloning parents were dealt with for not sending their children regularly to school : —Michael Rourke, labourer, Bewsey, fined Sc.: James Painter, tool maker, Haydock-et., fined 55.; J. Wright, wiredrawer, Oliver-st., fined ss. ; H. Sherwood, labourer, Gandy-a., fined 55. ; Joseph Kirkham, forgeman, Bewsey-rnad,fined 5. ; Alfred Birchall, labourer, Buckley- St., fined ss. ; John Gandy, broker and shopkeeper, Ellesmere-a., fined ss. ; Alfred Barker,forgernan, Oliver- at., fined ss. ; John Duffy, labourer, Dial-court, fined ss. Eliza Banner, Heath-side, Be. and James Devon, painter, Lythgoes-lane, fined ss. Mr. G. Riley proved the cases. FElDAY.—Before Mr. John White, Alderman Harrison, and Dr. Gornall. MiscsmiN-Fors.—William Hayes, for having been drunk in Sankey-st., and for begging, on the night pre- vious, was sent to prison for fourteen days.—Henry Mills, charged with begging in the Mill Stone Inn, on the pre- vious night, was sent to prison for a week.—Charles Groves for having been drunk and disorderly on the Ist ult., in Sankey-st., was sent to prison for a month.— Elizabeth Shaw, was summoned for having used threats towards Elizabeth Lee on the 11th inst. She was ordered to find a surety for her good behaviour, and to pay the costs. ALLEGED TTLEFTII.—Edward Percival. otherwise Foy, was brought up on remand charged with having stolen 911bs of horse hair, value £5 ss. 64., from the warehouse of James Toole, marine store dealer. He was committed for trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions.
