FOOTBALL.

Secretaries of Football Chits are requested to note that reports of matches riayed on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bowsey-street, Warrington, not later than tea o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.

RUNCORN V. ROCHDALE HORNS: A TEAMS.—Played at Runcorn, on Saturday afternoon. The home team completely overplayed their opponents, in every depart- ment of the game, the result being Runcorn 4 goals. 4 tries and 4 minors to nil.

FRODSHAX V. RUNCORN RECRRATION.—In stormy weather these clubs met at Frodsham' on Saturday, when there was but a limited number of 'spectators. The visitors, who won the toss, elected toplayivith the wind, which was very rough. Frodsham played with much dash, and cut out some heavy work for the Recreation, who, however, scored a try in the first half, to a minor by Frofisham. In the second half the home team pressed the visitors back, and Mereez soon got over, but the goal failed. The captain of the visitors lost his temper, and left the field with several of his men, the score being —Fmdsham, 1 try, 2 minors ; Runcorn, 1 try.

„ WIDNES v. MORRC.AMBE.—this match was played on the ground of the former, on Saturday afternoon, in very unfavourable weather. The visitors started the ball, but no return was made, and play settled in the home quarters. From a sPrimmage at this point Clarke ie- ceived a pass and transferred play to the visitors' territory, where, owing to some pressure by the home team, a minor was conceded to them. Howard subse- quently made his mark, and the place kick was taken by Morris, which fell short. A neat dribble by the visitors' forwards put the home team on the defensive, in which Stubbs and Farmer were conspicuous. The ball was gradually worked back into the,visitors' quar- ters, where Farrell got possession from sime loose play, and by means of some dodgy play crowed the line. The point was, however, disputed by the visitors, but finally allowed by the referee. Morris took the kick, but failed. The visitors now played with such determination that it appeared certain they would score, but disappointment was the only result. Smith and Stubbs were mainly responsible for bringing relief, and were gradually work- ing the ball into the visitors' territory when the whistle sounded for half-time, when the score was Widnes one try and two minors to one minor. Shortly after chang- ing ends Howard sustained injuries to his knee which necessitated his retirement from the field. In the re- !minder of the game his loss was keenly felt, and shortly afterwards Elkin ran over, but the try was not improved upon. After the visitors had made another futile at- tempt at goal from a place kick. Peters got possession and made a good run,but was eventually collared. Gor- don, who up to this time had filled the place of full back, was put amongst the forwards, and his place was taken by Farmer. Some tgood defensive play followed, in which Stu'obs, Morris, and Smith were con- spicuous and evidently Stubbs got away with a dribble. Athtow, forward, however, was penalized by a scrim- mage in front of the goal, from which Stubbs came forth with the ball at his toes, and with the assistance of Smith it was carried over the line, but was called back owing to some infringement of the rules. The visitors then repulsed their invaders, and compelled theta to con- cede a minor, the full back failing to put in his kick. At the call of no time the game ended in a draw, the score being Widnes one try and two minors to Morecambe one try and three minors. Teams :—Widnes: Gordon, back; Clarke, Morris, and Peters. three-quarters ; Howard and Farrell, half backs; Smith, Pearson, Farmer, Gandy, Holt, Tickle, Stubbs, Whelan, and Tonkies, forwards: umpire, Mr. A. Hufton. Morecambe: Dense, back; Miller, Elkin, and Saunders, three-quarters; Altham, and Woodhouse, half-backs; Cross, Altham, Holmes. Swain, Winder, Milner, Woodhouse, Burrough, and Archer, forwards; referee, Mr. Maclean.

ROCHDALE HORNETS V. RUNCORN. Nearly 4,000 spectators witnessed the return match between these clubs at Rochdale. Previous to the commencement of the game a violent thunderstorm passed over the'ground, and the turf was rendered aperfect quagmire. The home team played their full team with the exception of Nuttall, one of their usual half backs, and T. Melledew was brought out of the scrimmage to fill the vacancy. Run- corn also brought their best team, and Crompton, who played centre three-quarter, came in for an enthusiastic reception. It was 4.15 before Melledew kicked off, Brazendale returning into touch near the centre flag. Here a series of closely contested scrimmages ensued, both teams working very hard. H. Hughes was early prominent with a neat run, and judiciously put into touch near the home teim's 25 flag. Melledew, Mutch, land P. Ford relieved the pressure for a time, but the Runcorn men would not be denied, and Crompton punt- . ing over the home team's goal line, a minor point was registered after ten minutes play. Melledew dropped out, and after some give-and-take play, Crompton, from a lead kick by Barrett secured the ball very smartly, and slipping past T. Smith scored a good try. The place- kick, by the same player, although in a favourable position, was a failure. The Hornets' forwards led by Mutch, Brearley, Griffiths, and Sharp, quickly ran the ball down the field, and some splendid passing ended in Melledew scoring a try under the posts amid loud cheers, which were renewed when Lord placed the ball over the crossbar. Nothing further of nete took place up to half time, when the score was in favour of the Hornets by one goal and one minor point to Runcorn one try and one minor. Crompton resumed the game, and Mutch replied with interest. The game now became exceedingly fast, notwithstanding the heavy state of the ground, and the tackling on both sides was not of the mildest description. Mutch here met with an accident to his head, and was taken off the field to have his injury attended to, hut after an absence of some few minutes he was again able to take his place. From this point the game underwent a complete change. The Hornets fell away in a most unaccountable manner, whilst on the other hand the visitors' combination was grand. From a smart pass Crompton gained his second try under the posts, and easily landed a goal, which had the effect of placing Runcorn ahead. The same player five minutes later scored another try, and again placed a goal. Thisseemed to take all the life out of the home team, and Crompton for the fourth time ran round Lord and again placed a goal. Hastings next had hard lines in not scoring after a brilliant run, a minor accruing from the effort. Riley was next to score for Runcorn, but Brazendale, from a difficult angle' failed to convert, and a one-sided game ended in a win for Runcorn by 3 goals. 2 tries, and 3 minors to Rochdale Hornets, 1 goal, and 2 minors. Referee : Mr. E. H. Flower. Waimea-roe A v. Tusneome—Tnis return fixture, which had been anxiously looked forward to by both parties, was on Saturday brought to a satisfactory con- clusion on the Wilderspool enclosure. Although the first encounter between these two teams resulted in a win for Tuebrook, still the visitors fully recognised the prowess of their doughty opponents, and accordingly whipped together theirstrongest team, the names of the various combatants being :—Tuebrook: Bayley, back; Ellams, Eccles, and Morris, three-quarter backs; Bleasdall and Plank, half backs; Fletcher, Fletcher, Wootton, Pearson, Pearson, Ker, Weston, Jones, and Hewitt, forwards. Warrington : Boscow, back; Daniels, Speakman, and Lawless, three-quarter backs; Rowe and Mather, half backs; Nevins, Davies, Molyneux, Beard, Bate, Thorn- ley, Berry, Holmes, and Barnes, forwards. Tuebrook. winning the toss, Thornley commenced against the wind and rain, Nevins soon showing up by a dashalong touch. Morris passing to Eccles enabled that player to put in a tall punt, and Ellams quickly getting possession, ran splendidly to the line, a try being recorded. This early. reverse roused the home team, and after a capital dribble by Holmes, a spell of passing by Rowe, Speakman, and Daniels almost resulted in Berry scoring. A temporary stoppage of the game was at this part necessitated owing to Daniels being hurt, the oatcome of it being that Nevins was drafted to the three-quarter position. Some pretty play by Lawless and Neiins was neutralized by a flying kick from Ellams, and for a time the home team had to defend. Ultimately Nevins relieved to centre, and after a rush by Beard, Thornley, and Davies, some strong forward play by the visitors completely reversed matters, and Nevins saved what appeared to be a certain try. With only eight men in the pack, the home front rank played up grandly, and a screw scrinvnage somewhat re- lieved the pressure. The Liverpool team were now hard pressed, until Pearson put in along kick to Boscow, who 'replied to touch at midfield. Barnes shone next by a good tackle, and a fine bit of work between Mather, Daniels, and Nevins, enabled the homp team to again at- tack strongly, and Meilyneaux on one occasion snapping the ball up splendidly was almost over. The visitors again experienced a very anxious time of it, but Wootton from a line out ran finely to mid-field, Rowe stopping the rush daringly. This was responded to by Lawless taking the ball in fine style, and subsequently he ran strongly to the line, Bayley proving too sure to pass. Half time arrived with Tuebrook leading by a try. Changing ends and re- starting, Ellams early on tried to get away, but was stopped be Lawless, and following a piece of useful play by Bate, Tuebrook, headed by Ker, Weston, and Hewitt, dribbled down the field, Boscow, however, relieving finely, and a capital screw kick ify Speakman was of considerable advantage. Berry soon afterwards got finely away, and some passing amongst the home for- wards transferred the game to the visitors' line, Bate securing a try. Although the kick off was charged Bayley got the ball out of danger grandly, but Nevins by a capital pick up almost scored, a minor resulting. Soon after the drop out, some capital passing between Rowe and Mather enabled Daniels to run over grandly, no goal resulting, and another minor was forced directly afterwards. Restarting the game was carried on in a most vigorous and determined manner. In the mean- time a splendid dribble by Ker, Jones, and Wootton took the ball past the borne backs,but Speakman sailed round his opponents and kicked to midfield, where Daniels dashed off with a dribble and Thornley by a smart piece of work and kick took the game to the visitors' lines. A series of passing between the visitors was foiled by Nevins, and following some good work he Rowe a dribble headed by Beard, Berry, and Molyneaux gained ground. For a time the game was fiercely contested at midfield, but the grand combination of the home for- wards more than neutralised the weight of their oppon- ents. Not to be denied. Tuebrook again attacked, and Ellams from a miskick got a try, Pearson making a fine attempt to convert. Berry followed the drop out finely, and a rush headed by Davies, Holmes, and Beard was stopped by Bayley. Ultimately from a fine screw kick

by Rowe from touch, Thornley got a try near the posts, which Mather converted. Restarting, Nevins who played grandly throughout, soon shone by taCkling Eccles finely, and a fine kick by Speakman went to touch at the quarter flag, and the visitors after being pressed conceded a minor. Ultimately Weston got away strongly, but nothing resulted, and Warrington work after one of the most determined and hardest fought games korit- nessed. Score: Warrington, 1.2-4; Tuebrook, 0-2-0.

WARRINGTON V. KENDAL HOFCEI'S. After fortnight's absence from the footbaU field, the Warringtonians encountered Kendal Hornets in the re- turn fixture, which was set down for decision at Kendal on Saturday afternoon. The Warringtonians mustered a strong team, the only absentee being Nevins, whilst on the other hand the Hornets placed their strongest team on the field this season, evidently with the intention of reversing the verdict of the first meeting, when War- rington won. The day in the earlier part of the morn- ing was beautifully fine, but toivards the time for com- mencing the match-2.4s—rain eine down in torrents, a strong wind prevailed, and what promised to be a good match was somewhat hindered by the unfavourable state of the weather.

However, Warrington having won the toss, Wilson I started against the wind, and a display of exchange kicking between Berry, Bell. and Massey found play in the Hornets' twenty-five. Play was located here for a lengthened period, a long succession of straggling scrim- mages and line-outs marking the proceedings. At length a pretty piece of work between Bate and Antrobus took play near the Kendal goal, and Lawless had a shot at goal which went wide of the mark. Massey was in attendance, and Allan luckily kicked dead as the War- ringtonian was in the act of grounding. This piece of ill-luck did not deter the Warringtonians from attacking, for a dashing piece of play by Fair Turner, Dillon, and Donohue once more placed the homesters on the defen- sive. Relief was found in a dribble by Parsons. whose effort was negatived by a tall kick on the part of Evans. Give and take play' if a desultory character followed, and the ground which at this early period of the game was a quagmire seemed all against the Warringtonians, whilst Kendal fairly revelled in the dirt and mud. Armstrong made a desperate effort to score, and only the effective tackling of Massey and Evans prevented him. Both Bandies and Frank Turner put in some use- ful work, and from a scrimmage near the Hornets' posts Hind saved. Massey met the drop out, and Bell with a capital run and kick compelled the game to be contested at neutral territory. The visiting skipper became con- MiliellOUS with a capital tackle. and a long kick by Barnes being well followed up by Donohue, the home- sters once more defended. The visitors made strenuous efforts to score, but the defence was too good, and although Barnes raised the hopes of his supporters on one occasion, the oval was worked out of danger. Another minor fell to the Warringtonians' lot after a spell of exchange kicking. The oval was rushed down the field at a tremendous rate soon after the drop out, and from a pack• near the Warrington goal Antrobus and Bate passed neatly, with the result that the oval was kept travelling, th- Kendal line being reached ere Armstrong saved. Eventu- ally another minor accrued and a pretty run by Arm' strong soen after the drop out improved the Hornetsl position, Turner eventally pulling him up. Beard put in another good run and Evans at a critical moment ran round and wound up a brilliant , effort by kicking in touch near the half-way flag. A drop at goal by Allan sent the oval dead. Following the drop out Kendal held the upper hand, and a display of passing by Atkinson, Berry, Allan, and Armstrong reeulted in the hitter scor- ing, Bell failing at the kick at goal. Warrington seemed to realize their position, for on the restart we found them pressing the Hornets in a resolute style all through. Though they were within an ace•e scoring en many occasions, all their efforts were futile, and half-time arrived with the score—Warrington five minors, Kendal Hornets one try and one minor. Frank Turner restarted, and the Hornets, aided by the wind and some tall kick- ing by Bell, at once made matters lively for the visitors. Evans, however, was in his best form and repeatedly frustrated the efforts of the Hornets to cross the line. A free kick to the Kendal men from half-way was met by 1 Handles, and he in conjunction with E. Dillon, Povey, tate, and Barnes gained a temporary footing well in the homesters quarters. A vigorous assault was made on the Kendal goal and the excitement reached fever heat. Armstrong and Barnes exchanged kicks with advantage to the Kendal man, and some spirited play by the Hornets' back again placed the " wirepullers " on their mettle. Berry threw wide to Bell, who travelled at a good rate • along touch, being finally hauled in touch near the line. A series of scrimmages followed here, the monotony being relieved by a spell of short passing amongst the Kendal backs, Massey frustrating the effort by a capital tackle of Armstrong. .A screw kick by Barnes sent the oval to the half war flag where A ritrobus and Bate further improved Warrington's position, but their efforts were more than neutralized by a long kick by Hine, who deposited the oval in touch at the Warrington quarter Bag. From a pack here the oval was again passed to Armstrong, and Evans judging his man grandly a yard from the line, brought him down in grand style. The Hornet's representative, however, struggled on his knees over the line, and now came an unfortunate incident which marred the game. The Warrington captain naturally appealed against the legitimacy of the point, but judge of Turner's surprise when the official who acted in the capacity of referee, and who had given any- -1 thing but satisfaction to the Warringtonians throughout the game, walked away with the Kendal captain. This was too much for the Warringtonians, and although they persisted in being heard, they were simply ignored. with the ultimate result that Turner led his men off the field and resolved not to continue the game under such conditions. The point was so glaring that the players never dreamt that the point would be allowed, and as an instance of the unfairness of the decision, the Hornets' captain wished to have the leather played where the alleged infringement occurred, but as the try had been allowed, they (Kendal) had no choice whatever in the matter, and an interesting game was brought to an abrupt termination. Final score :Kendal Hornets 0-2-3. Warrington 0-0-5. Teams :—Warrington : Evans, back; Massey, Barnes. and Lawless, three-quarters; Bate and Antrobus, half backs; Fair. Turner (captain), F. Turner, W. Dillon, E. Dillon, W. Bandies, R. Littlewood, B. Eyre, W. Povey, and T. Donohue. Kendal Hornets :T. Hine, back; Bell, Allan, and Artnstrong (captain), three-quarters; Win- skill and Berry, half backs; Atkinson, T. Wilson, Heap, Beard, Simm, E. Wilson, Thompson, E. Hine, and Parsons.

div.p: DEATH OF CANON HOPWOOD, OF WIN WICK.

It is with regret that we announce the death of Canon llopwood, Rector of Winwick, an event which took place on Tuesday. at Winwick Hall. Since the death of his wife, Lady Ellinor Hopwood, in 'September, 1887, the deceased gentleman has been in a delicate state of health, but has gone about his duties much as formerly, and was present at the last ruri-decanal chapter, held in Warrington a few days ago. Mr. Hopwood was born on the 2nd of August, 1810, and was consequently at the time of his death in his 80th year. He was the son of the late Mr. R. G. Flop- wood, of Hopwood Hall, near Bury, and was educated at Eton. Subsequently he went to Christ Church, Ox- ford. He was ordained by the late Archbishop Sumner —then Bishop of Chester—in 1833, in which'year he also took hia R.A. degree. Ater spending a year with the late Canon Slade at Bolton, he went b Burnley, where for two years he laboured as curate. In 1835 he was appointed curate of Warrington Parish Church by the then rector, the Hon. and Rev. H. Powys, and there he remained five years, rendering valuable assistance in the foundation of the Training College and. the Clergy Daughters' School, of which for many years he acted as secretary. ' Mr. Hopwood was ap;. pointed first vicar of Knowsley in 1840, and be- came also chaplain to the Earl of Derby. In 1855 he was appointed rector of Winwick, succeeding the Rev. J. J. Hornby. In 1866 he was made Rural Dean of War- rihgton, and became Honorary Canon of Chester in the same year. Mr. Hopwood was married in 1835 to Lady Ellinor Stanley, daughter of the 13th Earl of Derby. One of his datzghtersis the wife of the Rev. J. L. Darby, Dean of Chester,. and the other, who is unmarried, lived with her father at Winwick. The eldest of his three sons is the Rev, F. E. Hopwood, rector of Bury. Major Hop- wood, late of the,Rifle Brigade, is the second son, and the third is Mr. C. A. Hopwood, one of the private secre- taries to Lord Salisbury. The living of Winwick has been for many years one of i the richest n England, the gross annual income being returned in " Crockford " at £3,500. A few years ago the Winwick Parish Act was passed, and its operations will besuch that the income of the new rector will not exceed £1,500 a year. Under the Act the ecclesiastical property of the parish will now be divided among the nine or ten parishes formed out of Winwick, including Ashton-in-Makerfield. Ilsydock, Golborne, Croft, New- church, Glazebury, and Earlestown. The living of Win- wick is in the gift of the Earl of Derby. ; The late Canon,Hopwood was a very successful and accomplished preacher, though of late years he had rare- ly occupiedthe pulpit. One of his last-discourses, if not the last, was on the occasion of the Jubilee celebration. It was printed at the time, and is considered to be a most able and vigorous production in support .of the Queen and Constitution and of Church and State. He took a great interest in all matters connected with the parish ;to the poor, especially the sick poor, he was a kind friend ; while with regard to the educational affairs of the parish, it may be stated that he not only built Winwick schools, but twice subsequently enlarged them, and defrayed all the expenses connected with them. He also built the school at Houghton Green,which he has also maintained for rrfanv years. During his residence in the parish the ancient church of St. Oswald was repaired, to the cost of which he was a liberal contributor. Into the history of this ancient church it is not now necessary to enter. It is well-known th there is a tradition that the church was to have occupied another site, and that after the building materials were deposited upon it they were tic some mysterious agency removed to the place Where the church now stands, while another story, says Mr. Beamont, makes a pig the good spirit which thus removed the stones, carrying them one by one round its neck to the new site, thus indicat- ing the proper place for the church and so helping on the work, on which account, it is said, this working pig is honoured with an effigy in the steeple. The deceased Canon tot* much interest in all matters connected with the Church, and attended most diligently the meetings of the Church institutions. From the year 1865 to 1883 he acted as rural dean. Although he had rarely occupied the pulpit of late years, his interest in the affairs of the parish had not abated ; and it is stated that only a few days before his death he was engaged in preparing about 30 young men for confirmation, his interest in the education of the children of the parish being as great as ever. The remains of the deceased gentleman will be in- terred at St. Oswald's to-day, (Saturday,) at twelve, noon, when the funeral service will be conducted by the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, vicar of Huyton (a nephew of the deceased and a former curate of Winwick), who will be assisted by the Rev. J. Carson, M.A., who for the last 13 years has been curate of Winwick.

FOOTBALL—RUGBY. To-day's matches :—Warrington v. Leeds Parish at Warrington; Runcorn V. Leeds St. Johns, at Leeds: Widnes v. Cromptod at Widnes ; St. Helens v. Bram- ley at Bramlev ; St. Helens Recs. v. Morecambe at Morecambe. Warrington will also meet Aspull at Aspull on Monday.

There was more than usual interest felt in the meeting of Warrington "A" team and Tuebrook on Saturday. The Tuebrook team had notbeen de- feated this season, while the Warrington second lot have shown great consistency in their play. The game was first such a one as might have been expected for two such well-matched teams, and although the Warring- t,onians came out successfully with a goal to the good the visitors did a good share of the pressing.

The encounter at Kendal between the renowned Hornets of that town and WarrinY,ton first team had an unfortunate termination. The Hornets have not done particularly well this season but on Saturday thoy seemed determined to turn the tide of defeat. They whipped up their strongest team and they played with the utmost determination. In addition to this tlwy seemed to have had a powerful helper in the referee, and one of the decisions of that functionary appeared to be so flagrantly unjust in the eyes of the" wirepullers" that the latter left the field and brought the game to an untimely end.

The latter had the most difficult task in getting through the falls. •On the way they passed men lying in the workings alive. but seriously hurt: Milk and brandy were administered to them, although the rescuers could hardly crawl back into purer air. The-operation of re- storing ventilation had the effect of bringiiag- out rest quantities of g,as into the Cribbwr seam; although an experienced nem pronounced that the 'seam was safe. The attempts., at rescue were of the most heroic charac- ter. .The thee parties of explorers were headed by Lewis Rees and Jones Williams, One went along- the airway and the other by the engine plane. itself. Those who took the latter route had to climb over several' falls, but both got to the bottom of the plena safely-. Here they found a heavy fall extending quite• eighty yards. div.p: ALLEGED ELOPEMENT AND ROBBERY.

Louisa Peters; a young woman smartly dressed. and Harry Millington, a tall, welt-dressed man, were charged at Westminster Police Court, on Wednesday, with steal- ing £250 belonging to Arthur John Peters, husband of the first-named, from his residence at Chelsea. Prose- cutor said he was formerly a steward on the Orient, but left the sea four months ago. He married the female prisoner in November, and went out on the sth ultimo to negotiate the purchase of a public-house. In his absence his wife disappeared, and he found she had gone off with Millington to Brighton. .He admitted that he left his wife soon after Christmas and stayed with another woman, but his wife asked him to go back. The accused were remanded on bail.

ASSAULT ON TWO ITALIANS

div.head: AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: AT WARRINGTON.

A DRUNKEN FREAK THAT ENDED SERIOUSLY. THE ASSAILANTS SENT TO JAIL. Two Italians, a box-organ, and a monkey, had a stuffing adventure in Manchester-road on Satur- daY morning, the particulars of which were related at the Warrington Police Court on Monday, by the Chief Constable and a number of witnesses. Four inen, named Bibby, who lives at the Packet-stage; George Machin, Priestly-street; Joseph Starkey, New-road, Latchford, and Thomas Ford, Marsh House-lane, who were all described as tanners and men of previous good character, were placed in the dock on charges of having been drunk and dis- orderly in Manchester-road, on Saturday morning, ci having assaulted Thomas Lanna and Luige Ran- I!etta, the Italians in question, and of having a,amaged a box organ belonging to the latter. The defendants were represented by Mr. Jenkins.

STATEMENT FOR TITE PROSECUTION. From a statement made by Mr. Hunt, the Chief Constable, it appears that there was an extraordinary rne in Manchester-road on the day in question. The Italians, on the Friday previous, came te Warrington With a box organ and a monkey, and took up their quarters at a common lodging-house in Scotland-road. Ou Saturday morning they set out to attract the con- of the Warrington public and as they were exhibit- Fig their monkey and playing the organ in front of some Liouses in Helsby-et., off Manchester-road, the defend- Walked up to them and began to tease the monkey. Tile complainants were patient for a considerable time, and endeavoured to prevail upon the defendants to de- k_aist. They, however, refused to do so. The monkey! rcame excited and began to screech, and the foreigners to shout. They resisted the defendants, blows were struck, and the complainants were knocked to the ground atV kicked. One of the Italians, the younger one, stuck the organ and the monkey, and the older man endeav- oured to push the defendants away. Blows and kicks Were given, and ultimately the elder of the two foreign- ,ers took off the handle of the instrument and struck at detendants, Ford and Starkey receiving two wounds each. Blood flowed freely, and the defendants then I:eade a determined attack on the complainants. The older of the two then escaped througha provision dealer's Shop into the back yard. Starkey followed, used very tiolent language, and seized hold of the woman the shop, hurting her arm. Starkey got into ire back yard, and the conflict was renewed in jr. Essenhigh's (mcnumental mason) yard, Mr. Essen- ogh having his head forced through •a window. 11:1, fermation of what was transpiring was taken ko the Police Station, and Inspector Spinks and several stables arrested the defendants,who were drunk. The ef Constable added that he had laid the most merci- charges against the defendants he possibly could; =9 might have been charged with a much more serious All the defendants were men of previous good • "racter, but they were "let loose" on this occasion; „_,t4eY got some drink and were therefore not them- waves.

THE EVIDENCE. It it Was decided to dispense with the evidence of the which would have required interpreting, and tmens who witnessed the 'affair were called. Maria ittlewood stated that on Saturday she was visiting her pl,lighter, who kept a provision shop in Manchester-road. 6aw the Italians with their organ and mqnkey, and • Just thrown them a copper when the prisoners came 0 and began teasing the monkey. They afterwards „Ped to take the organ from the complaihants. Because 7 old Italian would not let go his hold of the organ one ; the prisoners struck him and the others followed suit. le Italian struck two of them with the handle of his „earl, and then ran with his companion into Essenhigh's ba°elard. Prisoners followed them and beat them • 37. Complainants got away and ran into Mrs. Hare's • followed by the prisoners. Witae,ss endeavoured le Stop them, and Starkey struck her in the face. 11(.1'd tried to get his companions to leave the shop.— Weave said the elder Italian allowed one of the rt',Boners to turn the handle for a little while, apparent- tVaPing thereby to get rid of him. When, however, e Italian tried to stop him the prisoner, struck him a yZolent blow in the eye, blackening it. The other pri- ghtlers then set on both the foreigners and used them arnefully. She took the Italians into her house for 9tection, and when she attempted to prevent the '• sellers coming in they knocked her down.—Frederick :4seohlgh said that the Italians ran into his stone-yard oiazor refuge, and, because he got in the way and endeav- red to stop their assailants from following, the pri- ners knocked his head through a window. Ford was quietest of the lot.—William Davies, a Hussar. said VI witnessed the assault and did his best to protect the ftalians from injury. Fearing that something serious "uld happen he "took possession of a butcher's cart drove to the police station for assistance." Ford was ote Most sober of the prisoners.—lt was stated by one the Italians in court that the organ cost £l7 about 18 lactiths ago, and that it would cost £4 or £5 to have it Disellerly repaired.

SIR. JENKINS SPEAKS FOR THE DEFENCE. tMr. Jenkins addressed the Bench on behalf of his ients• He said that the prisoners had hitherto borne e most irreproachable characters. Starkey had been A 3.ears, Machin two years, Bibby five year, and Ford t:e or six years in the employ of Messrs. Tinsley, _ll,tlrers. Mersey-st. ; and Mr. Tinsley had writton res- Lr'',ug them, "I am astonished and annoyed that they iliould have been guilty of this disgraceful conduct." .kte,l3risoners had been working all the previous night. 811 o'clock in the morning they went out and had -sane _ pni oaer, Then at 8.30 they left work and, instead of rz,-404ff home to breakfast, unfortunately had some more If fr,i and that was the explanation of the whole matter. ha'ley had not had any drink that affair would never vh.°: "aPpened. They were going towards their homes they met the Italians and began larking with them. ooe they misunderstood the men's intention, and the rflan struck one of the prisoners with the organ enrsl-.ls. The blow was returned, and a general melee _,ed• The prisoners' conduct was, no doubt, most I,l'renensible, but he contended that the assault was of SO serious a character as it might at first sight 41,1)Pr, and he hoped the magistrates would feel that a ""erate penalty would meet the case. THE SENTENCE. ti 2120 Mayor, in giving the decision ot the Bench, said Atrj were exceedingly sorry to see four Englishmen al:„ding in such a wretched position. Englishmen iitZpi looked upon themselves as the protectors, in- ' be of the abusers, of foreigners. Drunkenness was sezies.xcuse whatever for brutality. They would each be arid' t° gaol for a month on the charge of drunkenness, po9 fOr a further term of two months for abusing the betr foreigners ; and, in addition, would have to pay ween them the sum of £5 and costs for the damage /40" tO the instrument; in default of payment another trith's imprisonment. In the case of Ford, who was eau°lsilte So bad as the others, the sentence on the second of tc' would be reduced to a month only.—At the close 'e business of the Court, the Chief Constable men- r,2_ed that the witness Davies had acted very well in the ;rtel: and it had jurt come to his knowledge that several tbeige Witnesses had been subjected to threats because of 'r evidence that day.—Alderman Harrison said it was tblrta, t contempt of court for anybody to hold out against witnesses who came to that Court to the truth and help to vindicate justice. If any cas, es came before the Bench, they would be -"'3' dealt with. MA PETITION TO THE HOME SECRETARY. tlq essrs. Jenkins and Unsworth, the solicitors for the witehtlee, have prepara.d a petition to the Home Secretary Eete,,,the view of obtaining remission of a part of the Tice on the grounds :—(1) That the punishment was tiffe""ive and out of proportion to the gravity of the ti„Tlees committed : (2) that the Bench retired to con- th'eerci their verdict before they had heard the solicitor for Of th:fAence ; and (3) that no sufficient proof was given t„-,"atriage done to the organ. A good many signa- - "aye been obtained.

The etiOrleer also sold the deceased'siron safe. Superinten- kid eahm just previously to the sale, opened the safe, toeic r• C. H. Pedley, the solicitor to the executors, Possession of the contents. The elder prisoner, Richard, was a dew_ in the Primitive Methodist Sunday School, right the f ,Ito the time of his arrest. He was also secretary of You:7 °°l, and is spoken of as a quiet, well conducted Be„:f This fact will be urged in his favour. The pri- cur' George also bore a good name in the village, but 'c't take any part in school or its connections.

trttrrs to tin Otittor. THE PURCHASE OF THE WARRINGTON WATERWORKS.

it a matter of necessity for the ratepayers of Warrington to purchase the Waterworks ? Before that necessity can be said to have arisen, it must be shown that the Water Company have fulfilled the obligations imposed on them by "..The Public Health Act" viz. I. Supplying the inhabitants of Warrington with a proper and sufficient supply of water suitable for all domestic and sanitary purposes, and. 11. the same to be supplied on reasonable terms. With regard to the first obligation, we have it stated on the authority of Alderman Burgess, Alderman Harrison, and Alderman Sutton in their speeches at the ratepayers' meeting that the supply was not sufficient for sanitary purposes, baths, or the quenching of fires. I think the official judgmentof these gentlemen on these points will be confirmed by the general body of the ratepayers. That the Waterworks charges are unreasonable any rate- payer can easily prove to his own satisfaction by comparing the price paid in other towns. Take Liverpool for instance. The charge there for water is at the rate of 6d. in the £ on the nett assessment for an abundant supply suitable for any purpose. In Warrington, the charge is is. 21d. per £ for domestic purposes only. We unfortunate con- sumers pay facl. per £ in excess of Liverpool for an inadequate supply, but we can console ourselves by the reflection that this aid. enables the directors to pay their maximurn dividend. To illustrate what I have said ;on a £6B assessment in Warrington I pay £4 is. Bd. a year; in Liverpool the charge is £1 10s. for the same assess- ment. I have, therefore, in four years paid £lO 6s. Bd. more in Warrington than I should have done in Liver- pool, and this for an inadequate supply. This scale of exorbetant charges is permitted. by the "Warrington Waterworks Act," and the majority of our present repre- sentatives recommend the purchase of the Company's property on the basis of revenue earned by these charges, and also ask our consent to their obtaining powers to levy these excessive rates for an indefinite period of The water supply fronrAppleton not being suitable for domestic purposes the capital there sunk has not proved a profitable investment to the Company, but the rate- payers are not only asked to pay the amount of capital thus badly invested, but to pay 30 years' purchase on it, as though it were producing the maximum dividend -allowed by the Act of Parliament.—Yours etc., THOMAS GREAVES. The Tower, Warrington, March 11th, 1890.

. MR. PEARSON AND MR. EMMETT. Sir,—Allow me to direct attention to a meeting, re- ported in your issue of the Bth inst., of the Newton-in- litlakerfield Improvement Commissioners. At the previous meeting of the Commissioners, the Chairman (Mr. J. W. Emmett, superintendent of the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Wagon Works, Earles- town), is reported to have charged Mr. Gillespie and my- self with going up to Euston, to make certain charges against him. At the Commissioners meeting of the 3rd inst., Mr. Emmett (in his capacity as chairman), stated that his remarks were not correctly reported, that " what he did say, or at least intended to say, and. what he be- lieved he did say, was, that Mr. Thomas Pearson, or at least Mr. Thomas Pearson's party had done so," and he declined to sign the minutes. Mr. Glover, one of the 'Commissioners, stated that "Mr. Emmett conveyed the impression that the" party "who went to Euston was Mr. Pearson's brother." The annexed letter from Sir Richard Moon will show how unfounded are Mr. Emmett's specific statements, and his insinuation about " going up to Euston." as affecting my brother, myself, or any 4' party" with whom we are connected. I presume it is the duty of the Law Clerk to the Com- missioners to record in the minutes the proceedings at each mAeting. Of his capacity and fairness in doing this there can be no doubt. Mr. Emmett alone impugned the accuracy of the official minute as to his first state- ment about "going up to Euston." The Clerk stoutly maintained the accuracy of his record of what Mr. Emmett had said, and was supported in his contention by several members of the Board,and I believe none but Mr. Emmett questioned the accuracy of the minutes. As to the legality of the wholesale excision of the minute of Mr. Emmett's statement (not on the ground of inaccu- racy but of irrelevancy) upon so important a matter I offer no opinion. As to the fairness and accuracy of Mr. Emmett's statements I leave the public to judge.—Yours obediently, Redclyffe, Newton-le-Willows, March 11th, 1890.
THOS. H. PEARSON.

(COPY OF LETTER REFERRED TO.) Copsewood Grange, Coventry, Bth- March, 1890. Dear Sir,-1 beg to acknowledge the receipt of yours of yesterday, and to say that what I heard about Mr. Emmett did not come from yourself or your brother or any one representing you.—Yours very truly. RICHARD MOON.
Thos. H. Pearson,

div.head: " FACTS."
div.p: " FACTS."

Sir,—ln reference to the letter of Mr. Robert Foulkes in last Saturday's issue,with your kind permission I will say a few words. Mr. Foulkes commences with saying "Samohtnede is still writing his ungentlemanly letters." I wonder what he means by this. Does he mean un- gentlemanly because of the rubbishy, reviling poetry written about our Bishop? Common-sense says "No." Mr. Foulkes being a scant (sounding, beg pardon) Protestant, delights to hear things said against " Ritual- ists." Or is it because Sarnohtnede calls Mr. Foulkes " Robert ?" Perhaps so. Mr. Foulkes is so very quick in this respect; but when it comes to some idiotic poetry written about our Bishop it is "well done." Perhaps he can say how long since it is that the late Bishop of Chester, now Bishop of Oxford, commenced to " s'A his face against Protestants." Is it since they have found out just lately (which they seem to do very expertly) that he is a member of the E.C.U., or one or two more such societies? Or is it by studying history, &c., he has learned that "Ritualism is not Romanism," the Church of England is apostolic? "The object of the E.C.U. is to bring the Church in union with Rome." This statement requires substantiation. I acknowledge one of the members said something to this effect, but such foolishness was very easily and speedily put down. some Protestants are ever ready to make the most of the least. "The Ritualists revile the Reformers," and Protestants do the same one minute, and the next it iS "the blessed Reformers." Whit shall we say about infant baptism, the sign of the cross, confirmation, the bread and wine being verity and indeed the body and blood of Christ (catechism), confession not forbidden (exhortation as to well receiving of the Holy Communion), ire., being in our Prayer Bonk (which has been declared by many to be Biblical truth). Let us not despise what little good we have. " Ritualists defy the law," and I would add Protestants break it. If the Church Association (where is the branch which was formed in Runcorn about two years ago ? ) were so ready to prosecute these Churchpeople, parsons and laity alike who say the general thanksgiving together when no rubric directs it (as in a church not far from MIIICOTTI, and dozens more besides) for watching a bis- hop celebrate the Holy Communion, and going there distinctly to watch him for lying on the pews when the Bible and Prayer Book tells them not to do so, as they sre to prosecute a bishop who happens to do tlaose things which his Prayer Book directs him, the church at large would be a little more satisfied. It is, therefore, plainly to be seen that so-called Ritualists are not the only law-breakers. If Mr. Foulkes, if he still be a Church- man, would obey the rubrics of his Prayer Book as laid down, one or two would spmpathise with him. What does he mean, I wonder, when he says, "They sympa- thise with the saints"? Is it a statement of the late Archbishop Whately's ? It is getting almost universal among the High Church clergy to teach the Priesthood of the Laity (bad job that). I refrain from saving anything about our bishop, not because "I prefer -olarkness to light" but that truth should not be exposed to error. I don't quite under- stand also what connection there is between so-called Ritualists and "by their fruits they are known." Oh ; I see, quite true, if we consider how many bishops, priests, and laity are members of the E.C.U. and other

societies, it is clearly to be seen that if this state of things continues they won't have any leaves or branches, never mind fruit on the Protestant tree. I would re- mind Mr. Foulkes of a statement made some time ago— " Protestantism dies hard, but it is dying." Mr. Foulkes, who studies greatly the religious events of the day can tell if this be true or not.
I hope I am not intruding on your valuable space.— Yours, Ste., . _ .
A CHURCHMAN.

div.head: Runcorn, March lth, 1890.
div.p: Runcorn, March lth, 1890.
ODD NATIONAL POVERTY AND GOVERNMENT EXTRAVAGANCE. HOW BRAVE/SOLDIERS ,ARE TREATED.

Sir,—Mr. Ralph Disraeli is retiring from his duties as assistant clerk in the House of Lords, for which he has been receiving for very light duties the nrdest sum of £2,000 a year, and with something like six months' holi- days every year; not a bad beith. But that is not all— his heavy labour and arduous duties have so incapaci- tated him for farther labour that a grateful country is awarding him a retiring pension of £1,500 a year. Who would not be a clerk in the House of Lords at £2,000 a year. with a pension in prospective'tof £1,500 ? I don't know what your readers may think of it, but this I know that many people say that it is a scandalous waste of the nation's money. This is one item. We have 64 generals and field marshals on half pay, 60 of whom are eligible for duty, but who do none, yet receive nearly £6OO a year while waiting for employ- ment. Besides these, we have 296 general officers on half pay, receiving £246,000 a year, or something like £B3O a year each. Thus while 60 generals are really wanted thereare 360 others to provide for in the shape of half or retired pay. It is said that the Duke of Cam- bridge is about resigningthe post of Commander-in-Chief, retaining the honorary Colonelcy of the Grenadier Guards, and £1.600 a year, besides the Parliamentary allowance of £12,000 a year and a palatial residence. It seems as if the government of this country knew no medium between recklqss extravagance and despicable meanness. Contrast the foregoing with what is to follow. The survivors of the Crimea, and the never-to-be-forgotten Balaclava Charge are, generally speaking, in extreme poverty. This is how they are provided for, these sur- vivors of the Six Hundred :—Private Brennan, 17th Lancers, is in a London workhouse; Private Marshall, who worked ia a machine shop at Lincoln till he lest three fingers is out of work and in extreme want; Pri- vate Holland, of Ormskirk, has no resources; Private Smith is a cripple and in the Strand Union, London; Private Burns, Trumpeter Brown, and Private Butler, are all aged and very poor; 13th Hussars—Privates Cooper and Mayhew, extremely poor; 11th Hussars Sergeant Brown, out of work and in ill-health, has is. id. a day: Privates Spring and Glanis- ter in extreme poverty; so is Private Richardson, who served 12 years. He has nqpension, but has Crimean Medal with 4 Bars and Turkish Medal. He suffers from stricture, and is nearly blind. Private Lawson, who lost an arm in the charge, is in the Royal Hospital at Chelsea by which he forfeits his pension. Bth King's Own Light Dragoons: Private Doyle, almost starving in Dublin, was Duke of Cambridge's orderly at Inkorman ; got £4 after earnest solicitation last year, not from the Duke's own slender pittance, but from a fund supported by public subscription; Private Rogers, helpless from age and disease, in Withington Workhouse; Private Keegan in Birmingham, very poor; Private Grant in the Royal Hospital, Chelsea, making two only of the survivors whose good fortune is to find shelter there; Privates Farrell, Carroll, and Brewington out of work and in great poverty. Yes, out of work! How can they work? They are old and what they endured in the Crimea was enough to incapacitate any man from work. Sergeant James O'Donoghue (Penketh) was born in the army at Canterbury, served as a boy 4 years in the 2nd Battalion 60th Rifles: was transferred in 1848 to the Bth Hussars where be had two brothers serving; was field trumpeter at the battle of A ima ; was field trumpeter at the light cavalry charge at Balaclava in which he and his two brothers rode knee to knee. He had his horse shot under him, and, after a very narrow escape, got back to his regiment; took part in the battle of Inkerman, the taking of Kertch and Yenikale, and present at the Tchernaya. He and his two brothers returned home with the remnant of the regiment in 1856 ; went out to India in 1857 ; was at the taking of Kootah and formed one of the flying expedition that for eleven days pursued the enemy who escaped from the fort of Kootah • was sunstruck on the march to Gwalior ; sent home and dis- charged in 1859, after 20 years' service, 4 years asboy and 16 years as efficient soldier, field trumpeter, and sergeant, wearing the Crimean medal and four clasps ; Turkish medal, French decoration for distinguished service, Indian mutiny medal and clasp for Central India. All this distinguished service has only been able to secure him a pension of Bd. a day. Who would be a soldier with a prospect of such, treatment as this? It is a workinitinan's question this. Does such treatment inspire patriotism ? Is there anything approaching to justice to those who have risked life and limb, and health in their country's service and then after 20 years' service as boy and man to starve on Bd. a day? It is simply a disgrace to the constituencies of the country that these brave men should depend on private charity to pro- long the remnant of life in a state of semi-starvation. Well may they cry" How long Oh Lord, how long ?" am, sir, yours respectfully, Sankey Bridges, March 10th, 1890.
CYMRO.

div.head: NEW BISHOP FOR DURHAM.
div.p: THE NEW BISHOP FOR DURHAM.

The Queen has been pleased to appoint Canon Brooke Foss Westcott, D.D.', to the vacant bishopric of Durham. Canon Weste.ott is Regius Professor of Divinity at Cam- bridge, chaplain-in-ordinary to the Queen, examining chaplain to the Archbishop of Canterbury, and canon resident of Westminster.

div.head: WEST HIM ATROCITY.
div.p: THE WEST HIM ATROCITY.

The inquest was resumed at West Ham on Monday, concerning the death of Amelia Jeffs—Joseph Robetts, builder of the houses in Portway, of which he house where the body was found is one, was recalled. He said he went over the houses in November with the police, as some lead piping had been stolen. He sent someone on to open the street doors, so he could not tell whether the key was used. Joseph Roberts, a schoolboy, deposed that he entered the house by the back window the day before the body was found. He was looking for a lemonade bottle, and he looked into all the cupboards, including that where the body was found, but he saw nothing then.—lnspector Wildey said a person could not see into the cupboard without striking a match.— Sergeant Forth, recalled, said the boy Roberts told him he entered the window with broken glass, but there was no broken glass in the back window. The jury returned a. verdict to the effect that the .girl Jeffs had been out- raged and murdered by some person or persons un- known.

THE PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED. At the annual meeting of this Company, held the other day, it was reported that during the year as many as 43,792 policies had been issued in the ordinary branch, producing a net annual premium income of £253,483. The increase in the ordinary branch premiums actually received (hiring the first three years of the present quinquennium amounted to over half a milliontand during the year there had been received the exceptionally large sum of £904,915. The claims during the year had amounted to £213,262, being an increase,of £3,200 over the amount in 1888. In regard to the industrial branch it was stated that the premiums received during the year were £3,336,742. The deaths numbered 150.557, an average of nearly 500 for every working day, which meant that every week the agents of the Company throughout the country had distributed to nearly 3,000 families thia sum of £25,000, at a time when it was most urgently needed, After the colliery accident near Pontypool, recently. thirty-seven claims were made for sums amounting in all to £5OO, which had been distributed amongst the relatives of thou who were insured and who lost their lives in that catastrophe. During the year the Corn- pant have issued 45,000 free policies. Insurers in the industrial branch, if they wish to discontinue their payments after having belonged to the society for live yean, can have a free policy granted to them for what they have already paid. TSe number of such policies at present in force is 171,316. The tetal number of policies in force at the end of the year amounted to over 8# millions, and constant efforts to prevent policies from lapsing have been unusually successful, for, although there were half a million more policies in force in 1889 than in 1888,the number of those which ceased to be paid upon was actually less than In the preceding year. It may be mentioned that the influenza epidemic has had a marked effect upon the Company's death-rates. Loadon was first attacked, and the epidemic afterward. spread throughout the United Kingdom, and is still very prevalent in the North of England, Wales, and the south- westbrn counties. The Company have at present only 652 cases where ithas been officially certifiedas the cause of death, but the proportion of mortality due to diseases of the respiratory organs has increased by 7 per cent. which is equivalent to an increase of about 3,000 deaths. They have also paid claims during the first eight weeks of tliis year over £BO,OOO more than was paid in the cor- responding period of 1889, not of course, all owing to the epidemic, as some allowance must be made for the larger number of policies; but after making this allowance the increase in the claims is put at no leas than £50,000. Further particulars as to the Company will be found in our advertising columns.

div.head: FATALITY AT BARTON.
div.p: FATALITY AT BARTON.

_ On Tuesday evening, Mr. F. Price, deputy dainty coroner, held an inquest at the Ship Canal Hospital at Barton, on the body of a man named Miles Whittaker (24), who lived at 17, Salters-lane, Eccles. . Deceased was a labourer employed on the Ship Canal Woilis at 'melt Park Cutting. At an early hour on Thursday morning he was passing along one of the railway lines. The morning was dark and windy, and he was blown against the engine " Weaver," which was going slowly along the line. He was badly injured, having several cuts on the body, and two of his ribs fractured. He was taken to the hospital, where he died on Sunday night. A verdict of" Accidental death "was returned.

div.head: NEW PLAN OF THE CANAL.
div.p: NEW PLAN OF THE CANAL.

A general plan, revised up to date, of the Manchester Ship Canal and the district through which it passes from the locks at Eastham to the Manchester and Salford docks has just been published. It gives an excellent idea of the country through which the waterway will pass,mentions all the places of note within a considerable distance, and clearly indicates the numerous intersections of the canal by road and railwaybridges and the Rivers Irwell and Mersey. In the estuary of the Mersey the low water channels and the sand banks covered by the tide at high water are shown. An enlarged plan, drawn to scale, presents a perfect conception of the dimension of the Manchester and Salford docks. There is also a longitudinal section, drawn to scale, showing the depth of the canal along its whole course. FATAL ACCIDENT AT LATCHFORD • YESTERDAY.

A man, who was known amongst his fellow workmen on the Canal by the alias of "Devon," was yesterday killed at the railway bridge which is being erected in Grappenball-lane, near Latchford station. A huge stone was being raised by the crane when a part of the stone near the "clip hole" gave way. The " clippers," opened, and the stone fell upon the deceased. He was , liberated as soon as possible, and conveyed to the WI) Canal Hospital. but he died in a few minutes after his admission. The deceased, who was an elderly man, was very badly crushed, but his injuries would have been of a more serious nature still had not the direct fall of the stone been partly checked by a wagon. SHOCKING FATALITY AT ACTON GRANGE. . .

A frightful accident. which resulted in the instantaneous death of a youth named Patrick Ccurtney,l.6 years of age, occurred on the Acton Grange secton of the Ship Canal op Tuesday. The deceased lad, whilst following his employ- ment as fireman on one of the travelling cranes, by some means or other accidentally fell between the cogwheels of the machine, his neck and chest being very severely crushed. Before the poor lad could be rescued by his comrades from his perilous position, death had ensued. Thebody was taken to the hospital at Thelma, to awaits the inquest. An inquest waq held at Thelwall hospital yesterday afternoon by Mr. Yates, coroner. Evidence was givgn which showed that the death was accidental. The only person who saw the deceased at the moment he was caught in the machinery was a man named Jones who was the driver of another crane about thirty yards away. A verdict of "Accidental death ' was re- turned.

div.head: CAPITAL OF THE COMPANY,
div.p: THE CAPITAL OF THE COMPANY,

It will be remembered that at the last meeting of the shareholders of tkir Manchester Ship Canal company the deputv-chairmari (Sir Joseph Lee), stated that it was the intention of the directors to deal with the remainder of unissued ordinary shares of the company, amounting to some £135,000, during the next few months, and that he thought he might safely predict that the shareholders and friends of the Ship Canal vrould support the directors in taking up some of those shares, time clearing off the liability which the Board had in the matter, and enabling them to issue the balance of the debentures. The entire balance of the unissued ordinary shares has now been placed at par among friends of the Ship Canal, without commission or discount Of any kind. The whole of the share capital having now been disposed of, the directors will be able to issue the remainder ef the mortgage de- bentures during the present year and in that issue the shareholders will have the preference of allotment. CRICKET CLUB* CONCERT AT THELWALL.

The annual concert in connection with the No. 6 District (Manchester Ship Canal) Cricket Club was held on Tuesday evening in the Coffee Room, Thel wall. There was a very large audience, the chair, in the absence of Mr. John Price, through indisposition, being occupied by Mr. Dix. An excellent programme had been arranged, the various items of which were admirably performed. The concert commenced with a duet (violin and piano) by Mr. Kessler and Miss Dix. Songs followed by Mr. R. Grounds, "Life is a River,' and Miss Ditch- field. "The Old Lock." Mr. Moore contributed "Good Old Jeff," Mr. Marshall "Sail Ho," and Mrs. Snell "Wishes and Fishes." Mr Beven very eloquently recited " The Fustian Jacket," for which he was warmly encored. The first part of the entertainment concluded with a comic song by Mr. Snell, who was encored. The banjo songs by Mr. Hownarn-Meek were much appreciated, and for his interpretation of "Go Home I Levi," he was recalled. An instrumental trio by Miss Dix and Messrs. Dix and Kessler was beautifully executed. Mr. Percy Davies's singing of "Quite English, you know," created much amusement. Mr. Snell was for a second time recalled for a comic song. Songs were also contributed by Mrs. Snell, Miss Ditchfield, Mr. Grounds. and Mr. Marshall, and a recitation, "Lady of Lyons." by Mr. Bevan. a most enjoyable and successful concert terminating with a trio, entitled " McMinnies' Band," by Messrs. Marshall, Robinson, and Threadeld, who were encored.

div.head: WEDDING AT GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: WEDDING AT GREAT SANKEY.

St. Mary's Church, reat Sankey, was crowded on Thursday morning, on the occasion of the marriage of Miss Mary Hatton, third daughter of Mr. W. J. Hatton, of Sankey Lodge, to Mr. Frank Houghton, fourth son of Mr. William D. Houghton, of the Beeches, Moore, and of the Sankey Wire Mills. The bride and bridegroom are well-known in the neigh- bourhood, and a large number of friends and well- wishers attended the wedding ceremony, which was performed by the Rev. E. S. Jackson (vicar), assisted by the Rev. T. E. Winder (curate). The bride was given away by her father. The bridesmaids were Miss Bessie Hatton (sister of the bride) and Miss Emmeline Hatton (cousin), and Mr. Thomas Crosby was the best man. The bride, who looked very pretty, was dressed for travelling in brown Irish poplin, and thebridesmaids,each of whom carried a beautiful bouquet, wore 'cream dresses, with .hats to match. As the wedding party left the church Miss Stanoish played the" Wedding March." After the ceremony the newly-married couple proceeded by train to London, where the honeymoon will be spent. As they left the church they received many congratulations, and the custom of throwing rice was pretty freely in- dulged in.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOONER FOUNDERED
div.p: A RUNCORN SCHOONER FOUNDERED

During Saturday night the schooner Eclipse, of Runcorn, sank in the Meisey near E:remont, after being struck by two heavy waves. The ferry boat "Snowdrop " was in the vicinity at the time, and tiere was no wreckage and no sign ofjthe crew. As the vessel was in a poAtion dangerous to navigation it was blown up on Wednesday by the Dock Board Authorities. The schooner, which had a carrying capacity of 160 tons, was specially bat for the Penmaemnaur ' traffic and at the time of the disaster was laden with stonq from that district, Mr. James Littler was the man- aging owner and the lose is estimated at £l,OOO. The crewe consisted of Captain Brown two men and a boy and it is feared that all hands were lost, as up to yester- day no tidings whatever had been heard of them. The foundering of the vessel is shrouded in mystery. _

div.head: WIGAN TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE WIGAN TRAGEDY.

On Thursday, the medical examination was completed and it is now positively proved that the girl Hannah Lydia Birchall was virtually outraged previous to her death. The funerallook place on Thursday. Thou- sands of people lined the route to witnem the cortege passing to the cemetery. Policemen headed the proces- sion, and one of two walked in the rear. The scene was very impressive, many of the female spectators bursting into tears upon the appearance of the processfon.

AT Trig EC-LICE COURT YESTERDAY. At the Wigan County Police Court. yesterday morning, William Dickinson, a collier, of Petticoat-lane, Ince, was charged with the murder of Hannah Lydia Birchall on the sth inst. The prisoner, upon standing at the bar, said. "I did not do it:" He was immediately silenced by his solicitor, Mr. Lees. Superintendent grassing- ton then explained the circumstances. The ell was left at home with the prisoner,on Wednesday: night week, and on the mother returning in about hait:aMtmar she was missing. The body was found on Sunday in a dis- used coalpit shaft 213 yards from the prlsoner'S house. The child had been violently outraged, and her skull was fractured. He applied for a remand until Wednesday 'next, which was granted. Mr. Lees raised no-objection to a further remand. The court was crowdedltb• excems. Prisoner-appeared pale and haggard.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION', It is now an assured fact that this election, will be. contested. The Owners' and Occupiers' Associa- tion intend to nominate Messrs. n. Carey, F: IL Gossage, T. Handley, S. Sadler (retiring members), and S. Owen (in place of Mr. 11. Gaskell, jun.) These candidates will be opposed by Messrs. W. J. Har- greaves, John Beech, and G. I. Neil. The eleotion takes place in the first week in April.

THtEs HEW, THOMAS CHAMPNESS AT RUNCQRN.. The annual sermons in aid of the Wesleyan Mine- Mitisionary Society were preached in St. Paula - chapel,. Runcorn, on Sunday, in the morning by the Rev..r.- Judson, and in the evening by the Rev. Burson.' On Thursday afternoon in aid of the same obj Ont,. the Rev. T. Champness, editor of" Joyful News" preached in the chapel to a good congrega...• tionl. In the evening a public meeting was held and the. spacious building was well filled by an earnest andattens, tive audience:. Alderman McKechnie of St. Helens,occhs pied the chair and he was supported on the platform by the Revs.. W. Champoess, H. Burson, W. Kendrew, J.. Judson i Messrs: John Simpson, T. Snape C.C., P. Speaks man C.C.,,F: Norman, and J. Unsworth. In the course of the proceedings the choir and congregation.. sang numerous, hymns with much heartiness.—After a brief opening, speech by the Chairman, the Rev. H., Burson read the report of the Home Missionary Society,, which showed,triat tnerer was a balance of £l5 3s. 4d. in. the Treasurer'§ hands, Last year the Runcorn circuit contributed the Ibllowing amounts. to the Society lection in classes, Sun- days, £l6 174 public-nieeting,£22 6s. 4d. ; Juvenile -£B,;. Congregational colleotion on Sun- Association at Camden, £l3 19s. sd. (Applause.) Sub- scriptions, £ll- Vs. 6d. total £6B Is. 2d., being an increase of I £2O -19 s, Wt. over the previous year. (Ap- plause.) The accounts- for the present year were not complete, but he might state that on Sunday last the collections amounted to-£.15 Is. 3d. • that afternoon £2. Ils. sd. ; subscriptions-R-7 as. • Camden Sunday School, £l7 15s. 9d, ( ). Mr. Snape, who had a hearty reception,. delivered, an address upon the need for home missionary effiert, end asked whether there were not living in the narrow boats in our canals, men and women who were veritable heathens, and living as though there were no God in the Universe. There was a floating population, about Run- corn, even more than. Widnes, upon the canals, who were living withoutthe slightests knowledge of these great blessings of Christianity which they professed to prize so highly, and it was the duty of the Christian Church to see that these people were reached some way or other. (fleas, hear.) And not only on canal boats, but on the fixed residences or the towns, were sin and vice at work. The reportsoltich- Mr. Berson had been kind to send him, stated thatthene were two reasons for neglect of religion for which the churches were not directly responsible, and one was drunkenness, and the other, the unwholesome and even miserable places in which vast multitudes lived, especially in the. large towns. He was, by no means certain that the church was not directly 'responsible for these evils. It was. aduty of the Christian Church to take these matters in hand, and to remove the causes which produced such terrible .results. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Snape-narrated some fearful instances of the great misery and: crime produced through drunken- , ness and said the evils could only be removed by , carrying into the midst of these people the influence of the,Crospel of Christ. (Applause..)—The Rev. T. Champ- ness, who was loudly. applauded, delivered a speech on home missionary.work„ in which he gave some personal reminiscences of his life and work. Alluding to the dreadful stories- told, by Mr. Snape said there were stories too bad to be told in nubile, both in towns and villages, and in the work of converting these people, they must have convictions as to what God said about the wicked. These people were wicked and they cold not go to God'S Heaven. They would spoil any heasfen they went to.. A. great many Christians had got some sort of notion that death was going to convert people. Nothing of thefl sort.. Death would not change them. They would have to start in the next world where tirey left off •' here. If Christian people only had con- victions upon this, £,ubject, they could do very ninch more than they did. (Applause.) Mr. Champness gave an interesting account a the rounding and progress : of the" Joyful News "Mission, and said they had made up their mirsdsto deliver the country from Popery, in- ' fidelity, and drihk„and by God's help they would banish the publio.houSes from the villages. (Applause). They could not spend too much care and prayer on the vii. ages of the land: eApplause).—On the propositionof Mr. P. J. Kerman seconded by the Rev. W. Kendrew, a vote of thankstwas accorded to Mr. Snape and Mr. Cha.mpness for the addresses anti a similar compliment was paid to the Chairman, for presiding on the motion of , Mr. P. Speakman,.seeonded by Mr. J. Unsworth.—Mr. Burson announced that the collection that night amounted to £27, an increase of nearly £5 over last year.

div.head: LIBERAL SOIREE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: LIBERAL SOIREE AT RUNCORN.

Thelilt• anima soiree in cbnnection with Run- corn, Liberal Club was held in the Public. Hall on Monday evening, and was a decided success. ,Mr. Brunner, She, m.r, for the division had, intimated hislntention to be present, but be was detained in London through his Parliamentary duties. The , proceedings commenced with a concert in which Mr. J. H. Greenwood of Manchester, took the principal part, with great credit to himself and amusement to the num- erous audience. In the sentimental "Serenade" On the humourous song he was equally at home, and in his character sketches he displayed talent of no mean order. He was several times encored. Miss Lloyd Jones contributed three songs in good style and was warmly applauded. Recitals by Mr. C. Conwaty 'formed a prominent part of the evening's entertain- ment. Mr. Conway displayed considerable elocution-. ary ability and dramatic force, and his various efforts were greatly appreciated. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys officiated as accompanist to • Miss Jones. During an interval in the " programme Mr. T. Clegg Came forward and in the name of the club gave all present a hearty welcome. He hoped if there were any young men present who had not yet joined the Club, that they would shortly have them, as members. (Ap- plause.) He had also to apologise for the absence of Mr. Brunner, who was doing better duty for the Liberals elsewhere. (Hear, hear.) An important division was ' pending in the House of Common% and Mr. Brunner as usual was at his post. (Applause.) They had arrived at a most important crisis in the-political his-ory of the present Government, and he believed that it was the beginning of the end and that they would shortiv have a general election. (Applause.) Amid applause-Mr. Clegg announced that Mrs. Brunnerand Mr. John Bronnerwere present, and introduced the gentleman to the meeting.— Mr. Brunner said he was sorry to have to apologise for his father's absence, but as all active publicans knew, that night, the House of commons had to express its opinion on the finding of the Parnell Commission. This was an exceedingly important event, and It would be a great breach of duty on the part of any Liberal member to be away from that division. (Hear, hear.) They ass Libera'sr could congratulate themselves upon the many events that were occurring in the polAical world, both I in and oit of Parliament. All things were going on as they could wish, and he referred with satisfaction to the recent election. (Applapse.) At the conclusion of the concert the room was cleared for dancing which was kept up until 3 o'clock the following morning to the strains of Mr. Wood's Quadrille Band. Mr. Joseph Pritchard was the M.C., and Messrs. R. W. Pierpoint and H. Wright, assistants. Messra.Spaning and Sons pro- vided refreshments, with the assistance of Mr. Oates of the Fleetwood Arms. A new feature of the refreshment room was a tastefully laid out stall of tobacco and cigars, belonging to Mr. R. Moore the hon. secretary of the club.

div.head: MPNDINO GREAVSTRIKE OF lINERS
div.p: MPNDINO GREAVSTRIKE OF lINERS

On Thursday a special Conference of delegates of the National: Miners' Federation was held at the arosvenor Hotel, ler Manchester, to consider the present position of the wages question, and the. refusal of the masters to grant an immediate advanee of 10 per cent.. Mr. B. Pickard, MY., president of theTederation, occupied the chair, and nearly 260,000 miners were represented, delegates being present from ever/ district belonging to the Federation except Monmouthshire and Stirlingsnire. The Chairman read a letter which he had receiWed from the Coalowners' Federation, lin which it was suggested that the whole wages question should be submitted to arbitraticn; but after considering the matter for some , time the Conference decided not to accept the proposal. , After a low discussion, the fallowing resolution was come to e,—." That, in order that the- present wage deadlock may pass away, we hereby agree that if the coslewners will agree to grant a. 5 per cent.. advance now and a 5 ;per cent.. adar:nce on the Ist off.naly, 1890, the present wage question be settled; but iffthecoalowners refuse to . grant the advance in this manner, the tools be brought • out on the 15th instant." Thb, Conference ad, Ourned until next day. DECISION OF THE f3ONFLRENCE. "1 Yesterday at the adjourned meeting of the Miners' ,Federation „ held at the Grosvenor Hotel, Manchester, a telegram was read from Mr. Procter Rhodes, secretary to Coalowner's Federation, who, promised tlr.t. the 'telegram sent by the Conference:on Thursday, should be Jaidlieforethe owners at their meeting on Monday next. ,The holding of this meeting on M.bnday seemed to come ,asa•surprise, and caused much discussion and specula- ;den. k reply to the following! effect was sent onthe :authority, of the president, Mr. Yickard, the vice-presi- alicl the secretary :—" As:, the owners' reply, is peculiar under the circumstances„ the owners must take full responsibility."—Telegrams :were also orderedlto be 'sent tothedifferent colliers in the country orderi:w the ,mente.throw down their tools end to go out on strike to-day (Siturday).

The proceedings by the Excise authorities against clubs in Liverpool for selling tobacco and intoxicating drinks illegally were continued on Wednesday. John Royce, in the case of a club called the Clarendon was fined in a total amount of £7O, and William Efaigh, Identified with the Chatsworth Club, was ordered to pay £3O. On Thursday about half a dozen of the club pro- secutions by the Excise authorities at Liverpool were continue& and In each case a conviction resulted. The fines ranged from £5 to £4O. . T ANCASHIRE EASTER QUARTER SESSIONS.— NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS OF THE PEACE for the County of Lancaster will be holden at the CASTLE OF LANCASTER, on MONDAY, THE SEVENTH DAY OF APRIL NEXT, at Ten o'clock in the forenoon ; and, by adjournment, at the following places and times, viz.: At the COURT HOUSE, in PRESTON, OD WEDNESDAY, the ninth day of April next, at Ten o'clock in the forenoon. At the ASSIZE COURTS, in MANCHESTER, 011 MONDAY, the Fourteenth day of April next, at Eleven o'clock in the fore- noon. The steamer Belgic has brought to San Francisco the news that 200 Chinese troops were recently surprised by 5,000 Formosans, who lay in ambush for them, and massacred every man. The authorities being without power to punish, the murderers made terms of peace with them. 416, SINGULAR POACHING CASE. An extraordinary case has this week been investigated by the magistrates sitting at Ashbourne, Derbyshire. At the last Derby Assizes four men were convicted of night poaching with violence, and each was sentenced to five years' penal servitude. It was afterwards rumoured that four other men living at Mayfield had made admissions concerning the affair which, if true, meant that the persons convicted were innocent. The upshot of inquiries into the case was the arrest of the Mayfield men, who have now been committed for trial.

- LABOUR AND CAPITAL. It is said that the proposal to establish a board of con- ciliation to deal with the more serious labour disputes in the cotton trade meets with the greatest favour. A Barnsley telegram states there is every appearance of a strike on a large scale by colliers, especially in in- land districts. There is again a strike in the Limerick bacon trade, the employefi !Irina refuß4 to take back the leader et the late movement. THE MOULDERS' STRIKE AT hOtTot4. This strike, now in its third week, continues without exciting incident. The rate of wages paid in Bolton is 365., and the strike is for a 2s. advance. THE BERLIN CONFERENCE. Mr. Burnett, chief of the Labour Department at the I Board of Trade, will accompany Sir John Gorst to Berlin, Ito assist at the labour conference. Sir William Houlds- worth, M P., will be co-commissioner with Sir John Gorst, and experts are to be sent to Berlin when techni- cal matters are being discussed. THE COAL TRADE. At a largely attended meeting of Yorkshire coalowners held at Sheffield, on Monday, the demand for an increase of 10 per cent, in colliers' wages was discussed. The present disposition of both parties directly interested in the matter indicates that a strike is probable. While uhcertainity prevails in this respect, prices of coal are going up all round. DOCK STRIKE AT LIVERPOOL. No work was done by the unionist dock labourers at Liverpool on Tuesday, and a procession of some 20,000 men paraded the principal streets of the town, headed by a brass band and waving banners. The shipowners, on the other hand, were working as best they could with the imported hands. About 600 men arrived in Liver- pool on Tuesday. The owners keep the men on various vessels in the dock, and they do not come outside. More steamers were working on Tuesday than for some days past, but the owners admit that the progress made is very much less than that by the regular hands. Two firemen named Dempsey and Martin, were each sent to prison for a month, with hard labour at the Liverpool Police Court, on Tuesday, for assaulting non-unionists. On Wednesday an important step towards conciliatory negotiation as to the dispute was taken, when the Mayor (Mr. Thomas Hughes) held a conference with delegates of the Labourers' Union. It is the desire of his Worship to promote arbitration as a means of arriving at a settle- ment of the question at issue, and the delegates under- took to lay his views before meetings of the strikers which are to be held this afternoon. Cardinal Manning telegraphed on Wednesday suggesting the formation of x board of conciliation, employers and employed, to select unbiassed arbitrators. At meetings held on Thursday the Liverpool dock labourers decided to refuse arbitration, and to go on with the strike "to the bitter end."

rpo NIGHT SOIL CONTRACTORS, FARMERS. CART- BRS AND OTHERS.—THE RUNCORN IMPROVE- MENT COMMISSIONERS are prepared to receive TENDERS for the emptying, cleansing and removal of the contents of all ashpits, cesspools, and receptacles for night soil, rubbish. filth, ashes, dust, Ac., within their District for a term of Three or Five years (at the option of the Commissioners), from the let day of May next, according to the conditions named in the specification. The Tenders, endorsed "Tender for the removal of night soil " to be addressed to the Chair- man of the Health Committee, and to be sent to the Secretary of the Commissioners on or before Saturday, the 22nd inst. The contractor will be required to find approved security for the due performance of the contract. The Commissioners do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender. The speciAcation may be seen and form of tender obtained onapplication to the undersigned. E. MARSHALL, Secretary. Town Hall, Waterloo-rd., Runcorn, March 6th, 1890.

IZUNCORN - CONTRACTS FOR PRO- VISIONS AND SUPPLIES, FOR THE HALF-YRA.R ENDING 29ra SEPTEMBER, 1890. The Guardians of the Poor of the Runcorn Union are dasir- ous of receiving TENDRILS from parties willing to contra*, for the supply of new milk, buttermilk, fresh butter and fresh eggs (for twelve months); flour, oatmeal, groceries, peas,cheese, salt butter; cod liver and paraffin oil ; quinine; good beef, to consist of vein and brisket pieces, the price to in- clude about 40Ibs per week of the best butcher's meat for the officers, and sides of mutton; best brand (lsts) American or English bacon; potatoes ; wheat straw, drapery and clothing; men's, women's, boy's and girl's shoes, of various sizes, as per samples to be seen at the Workhouse, Dutton ; house coal (colliery to be named); coke; good deal coffins, specifying size, and including plate with name, age, and date of death, to be delivered in the Union when and where required; carting at per mile, and funeral at per funeral.—Parties ten- dering for the supply of the above-mentioned goods, will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free of cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be ac- companied with samples (except drapery goods), as far as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter, to my office, in Frodsham, for a printed form of tender (and novo other can be entertained), where a schedule of the various articles required and further par- ticulars may be obtained. Sealed tenders, addressed to the Guardians, to be forwarded to the Clerk's office, Frodsham, on or before Saturday, the 22nd day of March, 1890, endorsed "Tender for—" The tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guardians to be held in the Board-room, Dutton, on the 25th March, 1890, at two p.m. Parties whose tenders are accepted must enter into a written con- tract, and be prepared to enter into a bond with two sureties, if required by the Guardians. By order of the Board, H. LINAKEit, Clerk to the Guardians. Frodeham, sth March. 1890.
